stem: Which of the following is indicative of a physiologic change of the renal system as seen in the parturient?
explanation: Glycosuria is common in pregnancy and should not cause alarm. It is due to the increased glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and the decreased renal tubular resorption capacity. During pregnancy, mechanical compression of the renal system and the effects of progesterone cause many alterations in the renal system. The GFR and the renal plasma flow are increased primarily due to a larger cardiac output. The GFR increases by about 50%, and when combined with the dilutional effect from the increased plasma volume, the plasma creatinine, and urea decrease. Creatinine and BUN levels should be lower than prepregnant levels, and values consistent with the pre-prepregnancy baseline should alert the provider of potential renal dysfunction. The increased GFR and decreased renal tubular resorption capacity make glycosuria a common occurrence in pregnancy.
rationales:
Due to the increase of GFR of about 50% and the dilutional effect of the increase in the plasma volume, both the blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine should be decreased. A level consistent with prepregnancy values could indicate severe renal impairment.
Answer B: Urea, uric acid, and creatinine all decrease in pregnancy as the GFR rises by about 50%.
bottomLine: Pregnancy-induced changes to the renal system include an increased GFR by about 50% with concomitant decreases in urea, uric acid, and creatinine and an increase in glycosuria.
references: ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Maternal Physiology: Renal" Miller's Anesthesia. Anesthesia for Obstetrics in Seventh Edition. Page 2206-2207.

stem: Which of the following statements best describes retinopathy of prematurity in the neonate?

options.text: Any procedures for treatment can be done with minimal sedation
options.html: Any procedures for treatment can be done with minimal sedation

options.text: Infants less than 1200 grams are at the highest risk
options.html: Infants less than 1200 grams are at the highest risk

options.text: The most cited cause is hypoxemia
options.html: The most cited cause is hypoxemia

options.text: The prognosis is poor in most cases
options.html: The prognosis is poor in most cases

explanation: Retinopathy of prematurity is seen in preterm infants, especially those with a birth weight of under 1200 grams. Blood vessels normally form from the macula towards the retina, which is normally complete at birth. In the preterm infant, this process proceeds for a longer period of time with risk of vasoconstriction, neovascularization, and hemorrhage. The most common cited cause is hyperoxia with sepsis, intraventricular hemorrhage, hypotension, and hypoxemia, having been implicated as well. Most will spontaneously regress and progress to normal vision. In the more advanced cases, retinal detachment and vision impairment may occur. Cryotherapy and laser procedures have been used with success and a general anesthetic is needed as a still surgical field is of extreme importance. During the anesthetic, a pulse oximetry reading of 96-99% should be obtained since the use of supplemental oxygen with readings in this range have not been implicated to cause additional progression of the disease.
rationales:
Most treatments require a still operating field and therefore a general anesthetic.
Answer C: While hypoxemia has been implicated, hyperoxia (too much oxygen) is the most cited cause of retinopathy of prematurity.
Answer D: Most cases result in spontaneous regression while some with the severe form have the potential for permanent blindness.
bottomLine: Retinopathy of prematurity is most common in infants less than 1200 grams with a most cited cause of hyperoxia. Most of those affected have spontaneous regression and a general anesthetic is necessary for treatment as a still surgical field is needed.
references: Barash Anesthesia. Neonatal Anesthesia in Seventh Edition. Pages 1200-1201. ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Neonatal Physiology: Retinopathy Of Prematurity"

stem: A 60-year-old man is scheduled for laparoscopic cholecystectomy. He has a 3-year history of diabetes mellitus as well as hypertension, treated with regular insulin and propranolol. The patient reports taking his medications before coming to the hospital. You receive a call from the nurse in the preoperative area that the patient has a glucose of 40 mg/dL. Regarding this hypoglycemic episode, which of the following is MOST likely to be seen in this patient?
explanation: Diaphoresis is mediated by sympathetic stimulation via release of acetylcholine and stimulation of muscarinic receptors and is the only symptom that may be seen in a patient who is hypoglycemic and on beta blockers. The normal response to hypoglycemia is an increase in sympathetic discharge, cortisol release, and glucagon release with symptoms of diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, altered mental status, and possibly even seizures. The sympathetic nervous system is composed of preganglionic neurons located in the lateral horn of the spinal cord from T1-L2. The preganglionic axons are short and synapse quickly in the sympathetic or prevertebral ganglia and the signal transmitted to the postganglionic neuron is through the neurotransmitter acetylcholine and nicotinic receptors. The postganglionic neuron then projects axons to effector organs and releases norepinephrine with stimulation of alpha or beta receptors. The exception is with sweat glands and the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, both of which are stimulated by acetylcholine via muscarinic (sweat glands) and nicotinic (chromaffin cells) receptors. The adrenal medulla is essentially a modified postganglionic sympathetic neuron. This patient is taking the nonselective beta blocker propanolol which will block both beta-1 mediated tachycardia and hypertension along with beta-2 mediated relaxation of the ciliary muscle of the lens which improves distance, not near vision. The parasympathetic nervous system originates from the brainstem and sacral spinal cord and uses acetylcholine at all synapses. Acetylcholine binds to nicotinic receptors at the autonomic ganglia and muscarinic receptors at the effector site. Answers B & C: This will be blocked by propranolol.
bottomLine: Sweat glands are innervated by the sympathetic nervous system and utilize acetylcholine with muscarinic receptors, therefore beta blockade will not prevent sweating with hypoglycemia which may be the only symptom seen in this setting.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Autonomic Neurotransmitters" Miller's Anesthesia. The Autonomic Nervous System in 8th edition. Pages 346-386.

stem: Which of the following BEST describes the Haldane effect?

options.text: Increased delivery of oxygen to metabolically active tissue
options.html: Increased delivery of oxygen to metabolically active tissue

options.text: Increased hemoglobin affinity for carbon dioxide in venous blood
options.html: Increased hemoglobin affinity for carbon dioxide in venous blood

options.text: Use of helium to deliver airflow to patients with asthma
options.html: Use of helium to deliver airflow to patients with asthma

explanation: The Haldane effect explains the increased ability of hemoglobin to carry carbon dioxide (CO2) from the tissues to the lungs for exhalation. Deoxygenated hemoglobin has 3.5 times more capacity for CO2 compared with oxygenated hemoglobin. Therefore, in the presence of low oxygen (O2) concentrations, hemoglobin binds more strongly to CO2, and, in areas of high O2 concentration, hemoglobin binds less strongly to CO2. Deoxygenated hemoglobin is a strong base that binds to hydrogen ions. In the tissue, O2 is released, and CO2 enters the erythrocyte. The CO2 combines with water to form carbonic acid by way of carbonic anhydrase and then ionizes to form hydrogen ions and bicarbonate. The hydrogen ion binds to the histidine residue on hemoglobin, while the bicarbonate (HCO3-) diffuses outside the erythrocyte. To maintain electric neutrality, chloride replaces the HCO3- (chloride shift). After it is in the lungs, hemoglobin is exposed to high concentrations of O2, causing it to have less affinity for the hydrogen ion, which is then released. The hydrogen ion then binds with bicarbonate to form CO2 and water. The CO2 is then exhaled and eliminated.
rationales:
The increased delivery of O2 at the tissue level can be partly explained by the Bohr effect. According to the Bohr effect, an increase in the CO2 and hydrogen ion concentrations will cause hemoglobin to have a decreased affinity for O2. This is seen as a rightward shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. As a result, hemoglobin will release O2 to the tissues that are metabolically active and are producing CO2. It is the complementary action to the Haldane effect. Whereas the Haldane effect provides an explanation for increased binding of CO2 for delivery to the lungs, the Bohr effect provides an explanation for decreased binding of O2 for delivery to the tissues. When hydrogen ions are in abundance, the hemoglobin has less affinity for O2 (Bohr effect and occurs in tissue), and, when oxygen is in abundance, the CO2 has less affinity for hemoglobin (Haldane effect and occurs in lungs).
Answer C: Helium helps deliver O2 to asthmatic patients in relation to the Reynolds number and the increase in laminar vs turbulent flow. When a patient has an asthma attack, obstruction to airflow results in turbulence and restricted flow to the lungs. Laminar flow is more efficient, and the Reynolds number helps predict whether airflow will be turbulent or laminar. The Reynolds number is determined by inertial forces (velocity, density, and length) divided by viscous forces. Flow is more likely to be turbulent and ineffectual when the Reynolds number is greater. Helium is less dense than nitrogen, and, by combining helium with oxygen, the density of the gas decreases. As the Reynolds number decreases, the airflow is more likely to be laminar, thus improving ventilation in the lungs.
bottomLine: The Bohr and Haldane effects are complementary principles that help explain the efficient delivery of O2 to the tissue and of CO2 to the lungs. According to the Bohr effect, in areas of high CO2, the hemoglobin has less affinity for O2, which is more readily released for consumption by the tissues. According to the Haldane effect, deoxygenated hemoglobin has a higher affinity for CO2. After the deoxygenated hemoglobin reaches the lungs, the high O2 concentration decreases this affinity, and the CO2 is released.

stem: Which of the following is MOST TRUE regarding balanced crystalloid solutions such as lactated Ringer's solution?

options.text: Most contain the organic buffer sodium bicarbonate
options.html: Most contain the organic buffer sodium bicarbonate

options.text: There is a transient suppression of anti-diuretic hormone secretion after administration
options.html: There is a transient suppression of anti-diuretic hormone secretion after administration

options.text: They have a higher chloride concentration than 0.9% sodium chloride
options.html: They have a higher chloride concentration than 0.9% sodium chloride

options.text: They have a higher overall osmolarity than 0.9% sodium chloride
options.html: They have a higher overall osmolarity than 0.9% sodium chloride

explanation: Most currently available balanced crystalloid solutions, including lactated Ringer solution, have an osmolality of around 260 - 270 mOsm/kg which is slightly lower than a normal plasma osmolality (285 mOsm/kg). Administration of these hypotonic solutions to a patient will transiently decrease the plasma tonicity and therefore suppress anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) secretion. This results in a temporary increase in diuresis in response to the increased intravascular volume. The term "Balanced Crystalloid Solution" refers to a crystalloid solution that attempts to mimic the normal physiologic makeup of plasma. This is typically done through the use of more physiologically normal levels of sodium and chloride (the major strong ions in plasma), as well as the other strong ions including potassium, calcium, magnesium, and lactate. In general, a strong ion difference is calculated as the difference between the serum cations and anions. Specifically, it is the difference of (Sodium + Potassium + Calcium + Magnesium) and (Chloride + Lactate). A physiologic strong ion difference is around positive 40 to 45. This is in stark contrast to 0.9% sodium chloride solution that has a strong ion difference of 0 (154 mEq/L sodium - 154 mEq/L chloride). Excessive administration of this hypertonic solution results in a hyperchloremic acidosis as the plasma strong ion difference is brought down. stem: Which of the following statements is MOST TRUE regarding neurotransmission within the autonomic nervous system?

options.text: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors are found exclusively in the parasympathetic nervous system
options.html: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors are found exclusively in the parasympathetic nervous system

options.text: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are found in the ganglia of both the sympathetic and the parasympathetic systems
options.html: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are found in the ganglia of both the sympathetic and the parasympathetic systems

options.text: Select postganglionic neurons in the parasympathetic nervous system release epinephrine
options.html: Select postganglionic neurons in the parasympathetic nervous system release epinephrine

options.text: The parasympathetic nervous system tends to have an inhibitory effect on the end organs of the body
options.html: The parasympathetic nervous system tends to have an inhibitory effect on the end organs of the body

explanation: The ganglia in which the presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons of both the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems synapse contain exclusively nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. As a rule, the autonomic nervous system (ANS) exerts its effects throughout the body through the neurotransmission of only three substances: acetylcholine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine. Depending on the tissue in which these substances are deposited, the ANS can have an inhibitory or excitatory effect which is mediated by the specific type and characteristics of the conjugate receptors within these tissues. Muscarinic and adrenergic receptors are coupled directly to G-proteins that allow these neurotransmitters to exert their end-organ effect through second-messenger signaling. Nicotinic receptors on the other hand directly cause an increase in the permeability of a cell membrane to sodium and calcium ions due to their direct association with the relevant ion channels and result in the rapid depolarization of the postsynaptic cell. Given these characteristics, it follows then that nicotinic receptors tend to be found in the postsynaptic membrane synapses when the effect of the postsynaptic tissue is to rapidly depolarize. An example of this is within the autonomic ganglia where the binding of acetylcholine that is released from presynaptic neurons to the postsynaptic nicotinic receptors results in depolarization of the postsynaptic neuron. Another example of where nicotinic receptors cause depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane is at the motor-end plate where their activation results in depolarization and contraction of the muscle tissue. Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors tend to be found in the effector tissues that respond to the release of acetylcholine from postsynaptic parasympathetic neurons. The notable exception to this is that eccrine sweat glands are innervated by the sympathetic nervous system and are stimulated through activation of sympathetically released acetylcholine that activates muscarinic receptors in these sweat gland tissues. Due to their association with G-proteins, the downstream effects that are caused by the activation of muscarinic receptors are varied. In some tissues this effect is excitatory (e.g. muscarinic activation of the bronchospasm reflex) and in some tissues it is inhibitory (e.g. bradycardia from muscarinic stimulation of the sinoatrial node). The release of the catecholamines epinephrine and norepinephrine from postganglionic sympathetic neurons tend to have predictable effects based upon the receptors that are being stimulated in the effector organ.
rationales:
Muscarinic receptors are found primarily in the parasympathetic nervous system, however, the sympathetically innervated sweat glands also utilize these receptors.
Answer C: The parasympathetic postganglionic neurons exclusively release acetylcholine at the site of their effector tissues which will bind to muscarinic receptors on those tissues.
Answer D: The parasympathetic nervous system can have either an inhibitory or excitatory effect depending on the effector tissue that it is innervating. For instance, an increase in parasympathetic tone in the lungs results in bronchoconstriction while the same results in bradycardia and myocardial depression in the heart.
bottomLine: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are found within the autonomic ganglia and at the neuromuscular end-plate and allow for rapid depolarization of the post-synaptic tissue. The effects that occur following the stimulation of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors are much more varied and depend on the second-messenger G-protein coupled reactions that are triggered by their stimulation.

stem: Which of the following would be most likely to DECREASE coronary perfusion to the left ventricle, without significantly affecting coronary perfusion to the right ventricle?
explanation: The left ventricle (LV) is more sensitive than the right to ischemia due to an imbalance of oxygen supply/demand to the myocardium. Decreased diastolic time mostly affects the LV, which is perfused primarily during diastole. Coronary blood flow is directly proportional to coronary perfusion pressure (CPP) and inversely proportional to vascular resistance. Resistance is defined by the Hagen-Poiseuille Equation, R = (8 * L * η ) / (π * r^4), where R = resistance, L = length, η = blood viscosity, and r = vessel radius. This law explains the marked influence of the radius on coronary flow (e.g. atherosclerosis). Left ventricle coronary perfusion occurs primarily during diastole because this is when aortic blood pressure is greater than left ventricular (LV) pressure. During systole, left ventricular pressure is higher than aortic pressure and there is absence or even reversal of flow in the coronary arteries. Because of this LV CPP is defined as diastolic arterial pressure minus left ventricular end-diastolic pressure. Increased time in diastole (e.g. with beta-blockers) will, therefore, increase left ventricle coronary perfusion. Right ventricle (RV) coronary perfusion normally occurs throughout the cardiac cycle because right ventricle pressure does not normally exceed systemic pressures. In an individual with aortic pressures of 120/70 mmHg and RV pressures of 25/5 mmHg, the CPP will be greater in systole (120-25 = 95) than in diastole (70-5 = 65). Because of this, coronary flow to the right ventricle, measured in mL/min, is greater during systole than diastole. Answers B & C: Higher filling pressures and lower diastolic blood pressure would decrease diastolic coronary perfusion to both ventricles, not just the left ventricle. Granted, this would be less taxing to the right ventricle because it is also perfused during systole, and also because it has a greater ability to increase its oxygen extraction ratio and to downregulate its metabolic demand compared to the left ventricle.
rationales: The right coronary artery and its branches have the highest incidence of vasospasm. Thus, Prinzmetal angina would not be likely to affect the LV while sparing the RV.
bottomLine: Coronary perfusion occurs primarily during diastole and is dependent on coronary perfusion pressure and vascular resistance. Coronary perfusion pressure is defined as diastolic aortic pressure minus left ventricular end-diastolic pressure.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding the upper extremity sympathetic nervous system is LEAST likely true?

options.text: Afferent pain fibers travel with postganglionic nerves of the upper extremity
options.html: Afferent pain fibers travel with postganglionic nerves of the upper extremity

options.text: Nicotinic receptors are located within the cervicothoracic ganglion
options.html: Nicotinic receptors are located within the cervicothoracic ganglion

options.text: Preganglionic nerve fibers originate in the lower cervical spinal segments
options.html: Preganglionic nerve fibers originate in the lower cervical spinal segments

options.text: Preganglionic nerve fibers synapse within the inferior cervical ganglion
options.html: Preganglionic nerve fibers synapse within the inferior cervical ganglion

explanation: Preganglionic nerve fibers of the upper extremity originate from the first four or five thoracic spinal segments. The cervical spinal roots do not contribute to the sympathetic nervous system. Nerves of the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) arise from the thoracolumbar segments (T1-L3) of the spinal cord. Preganglionic fibers exit the spinal cord via the ventral horn and form the white communicating rami to enter one of 22 paired paravertebral ganglia. After entering their respective ganglion, fibers can either synapse with postganglionic fibers at that level, travel up or down the SNS chain to synapse at a different level, or they can travel a variable distance to a visceral collateral ganglion. Sympathetic nerve fibers of the upper extremity originate from the first four or five thoracic spinal segments. These preganglionic fibers enter three different ganglia termed the superior cervical, middle cervical, and the stellate ganglia. The stellate ganglion is also known as the cervicothoracic ganglion as it is formed by fusion of the inferior cervical and the first thoracic SNS ganglia. Within these ganglia, preganglionic fibers synapse at nicotinic receptors utilizing the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. The postganglionic fibers then travel with afferent pain fibers to the head, neck, upper extremities, heart, and lungs. The widespread sympathetic distribution of fibers accounts for pain in the neck and upper extremity that can be experienced with myocardial ischemia. This also accounts for the efficacy of stellate ganglion block in conditions involving sympathetically mediated pain such as complex regional pain syndrome of the upper extremity. Answers A & B & D: This is a correct statement.
bottomLine: The sympathetic nervous system of the upper extremity originates from the first four or five thoracic spinal segments. These preganglionic fibers synapse via acetylcholine-mediated nicotinic receptors in the superior cervical, middle cervical, and stellate ganglia. Postganglionic fibers then travel with afferent pain fibers to the head, neck, upper extremity, heart, and lungs.
trueLearnInsight: Sweat gland activation by the sympathetic nervous system is unique in that neurotransmission occurs via postganglionic fibers utilizing acetylcholine instead of norepinephrine.
references: Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 7th Edition. Pages 364-366. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Autonomic Innervation: Upper Extremity (B)"

stem: An action potential at the muscle postsynaptic membrane is triggered through a sequence of events. Which of the following molecules is most involved in the first step of generating an action potential in a postsynaptic neuromuscular neuron?
explanation: When the presynaptic terminal is depolarized by an action potential, calcium channels open, resulting in an influx of calcium that triggers acetylcholine release. Potassium channels then open which allow for an efflux of potassium which rapidly restores the membrane potential. Meanwhile, the released acetylcholine travels across the cleft to bind to acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane which results in depolarization of the endplate. This depolarization opens sodium channels which generate an action potential in the muscle. Figure: The action potential travels along the presynaptic neuron to the presynaptic terminal, which leads to intracellular calcium influx. The influx of calcium causes acetylcholine vesicles to adhere to the presynaptic terminal membrane. After the acetylcholine molecule is released across the synaptic cleft, it binds to the central ion channel, which causes a net inward flux of sodium, which then allows for muscle contraction to occur.
rationales:
Potassium ions restore the membrane potential of the presynaptic terminal and are less closely associated with generation of the postsynaptic membrane end plate potential that triggers an action potential than sodium.
Answer C: Calcium ions trigger acetylcholine release and are less closely associated with generation of the postsynaptic membrane end plate potential that triggers an action potential than sodium.
bottomLine: The opening of sodium channels on the postsynaptic terminal triggers an action potential.
trueLearnInsight: The voltage gated sodium channel can be in one of three states: open (excited), inactivated (desensitized), or closed (resting).

stem: Which of the following is a source of tissue hypoxia from carbon monoxide poisoning?

options.text: Left shift of the oxygen hemoglobin dissociation curve
options.html: Left shift of the oxygen hemoglobin dissociation curve

explanation: Tissue hypoxia from carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning can occur due to a left shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. This occurs as a result of hemoglobin’s (Hb) increased affinity for CO as compared with oxygen. This leftward shift therefore increases oxygen binding to the Hb molecule. Carbon monoxide poisoning is commonly associated with burn victims due to smoke exposure during a fire. Carbon monoxide has an affinity for Hb that is 200-300 times stronger than oxygen. Hemoglobin preferentially binds to CO (carboxyhemoglobin, or COHb) leaving less Hb available for oxygen to bind. In addition, oxygen that binds with Hb tends not to dissociate from Hb, resulting in a leftward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. CO disrupts mitochondrial function, which leads to less adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production as a result of uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation. The inability to utilize the electron transport chain shifts cellular metabolism towards glycolysis and lactate production. Combined, these factors result in tissue hypoxia and a metabolic acidosis (with an anion gap). Clinically, CO poisoning is difficult to discover without an adequate history because oxygen saturation is usually normal. Standard pulse oximetry is unable to distinguish between COHb and oxyhemoglobin as they both absorb light at similar frequencies. The diagnosis of carbon monoxide poisoning is made by co-oximetry, when elevated levels of COHb (> 15%) are found on arterial or venous blood gas analysis. Treatment includes high FiO2 which helps displace CO. Hyperbaric oxygen is reserved for patients with COHb > 30% and/or severe symptomatology (e.g., obtundation, delirium, bradyarrhythmia, etc.).
rationales:
CO disrupts mitochondrial function, leading to less ATP production due to uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation.
Answer C: The inability to utilize the electron transport chain shifts cellular metabolism towards glycolysis and lactate production.
bottomLine: Carbon monoxide poisoning causes tissue hypoxia and acidosis by decreased coupling of oxidative phosphorylation, a leftward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, decreased ATP production, and increased lactate production.

This leftward shift therefore increases oxygen binding to the Hb molecule. Carbon monoxide poisoning is commonly associated with burn victims due to smoke exposure during a fire.

Carbon monoxide has an affinity for Hb that is 200-300 times stronger than oxygen. Hemoglobin preferentially binds to CO (carboxyhemoglobin, or COHb) leaving less Hb available for oxygen to bind.

In addition, oxygen that binds with Hb tends not to dissociate from Hb, resulting in a leftward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. CO disrupts mitochondrial function, which leads to less adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production as a result of uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation.

The inability to utilize the electron transport chain shifts cellular metabolism towards glycolysis and lactate production. Combined, these factors result in tissue hypoxia and a metabolic acidosis (with an anion gap).

Clinically, CO poisoning is difficult to discover without an adequate history because oxygen saturation is usually normal. Standard pulse oximetry is unable to distinguish between COHb and oxyhemoglobin as they both absorb light at similar frequencies.

The diagnosis of carbon monoxide poisoning is made by co-oximetry, when elevated levels of COHb (> 15%) are found on arterial or venous blood gas analysis. Treatment includes high FiO2 which helps displace CO.

Hyperbaric oxygen is reserved for patients with COHb > 30% and/or severe symptomatology (e.g., obtundation, delirium, bradyarrhythmia, etc.).
rationalesHtml:
• Answer A: CO disrupts mitochondrial function, leading to less ATP production due to uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation.
  • Answer C: The inability to utilize the electron transport chain shifts cellular metabolism towards glycolysis and lactate production.
bottomLineHtml: Carbon monoxide poisoning causes tissue hypoxia and acidosis by decreased coupling of oxidative phosphorylation, a leftward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, decreased ATP production, and increased lactate production.

stem: The following measurements are obtained during a cardiac catheterization. Heart rate 78 Arterial blood pressure 120/90 mm Hg Right atrial pressure 5 mm Hg Pulmonary artery pressure 24/12 mm Hg Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure 8 mm Hg Cardiac output 5 L/min SaO2 97% SvO2 72% What is this patient’s systemic vascular resistance?
explanation: This patient’s systemic vascular resistance (SVR) is calculated to be 1520 dynes * sec/cm^5. First, mean arterial pressure (MAP) must be calculated since it is not given directly: MAP = [(1/3) * systolic pressure] + [(2/3) * diastolic pressure] = [(1/3) * 120 mm Hg] + [(2/3) * 90 mm Hg] = 100 mm Hg Next, SVR can be calculated using the following formula: SVR = [80 * (MAP – RAP)] ÷ CO = [80 * (100 – 5)] ÷ 5 = 1520 dynes * sec/cm^5 Where: MAP = mean arterial pressure (mm Hg) RAP = right atrial pressure (mm Hg), central venous pressure is commonly substituted for RAP CO = cardiac output (L/min) 80 = conversion factor which changes mm Hg/L/min (Woods unit) to dynes * sec/cm^5 Answers A & C & D: This patient’s systemic vascular resistance (SVR) is calculated to be 1520 dynes * sec/cm^5.

stem: A 40-year-old female with severe depression is scheduled to begin electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). Which of the following is the LEAST likely response to ECT?
explanation: ECT is known to cause an increase in intracranial pressure (ICP) and cerebral blood flow (CBF), which is of concern in patients with space-occupying lesions. Intracranial lesions are a relative contraindication to ECT. ECT involves placement of scalp electrodes to deliver an electrical stimulus to induce a seizure of at least 25-second duration. Physiologic effects of ECT include an increase in CMRO2, CBF, and ICP initially, followed by a return to baseline in the post-ictal period. There is also autonomic stimulation with initial bradycardia followed by hypertension and tachycardia, which can induce cardiac ischemia. In fact, cardiac-related events are the leading cause of death after ECT, though this is rare. Side effects of ECT include headache, myalgia, nausea, status epilepticus (though it is also used to treat this), fractures, emergence agitation, and neurocognitive impairment. Both long- and short-term memory loss have been produced by ECT and can persist. However, short-term memory loss is more common. Studies have suggested that technical implementation of ECT can affect neurocognitive side effects notably that the use of short pulse, right-unilateral, non-sine wave pulses result in a more favorable side effect profile. Answers A & D: Both bradycardia and tachycardia commonly occur during ECT. Initial short-lived bradycardia is commonly followed by tachycardia.
rationales: Short-term memory loss is common. Long-term memory loss is also seen with ECT, though it is uncommon.
bottomLine: Physiologic responses to ECT include elevations in CBF and ICP, long and short-term memory loss, and autonomic stimulation with initial bradycardia, followed by hypertension and tachycardia.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "ECT Side Effects" Clinical Anesthesia. Electroconvulsive Therapy in 7th edition. Page 887. Prudic et al. Electroconvulsive Therapy Part I: A Perspective on the Evolution and Current Practice of ECT, J of Psychiat Pract. 2009 Sep; 15(5): 346-368.

explanation: Hypoxic patients (SpO2 < 94%) presenting with an ischemic stroke should receive supplemental oxygen to increase oxygen delivery to the affected area and also because these patients are at high risk for airway compromise. Hyperoxia should be avoided as well, thus oxygen should be titrated to maintain SpO2 < 100%, giving a goal range of 94-99%. Strokes or cerebrovascular accidents (CVAs) are a leading cause of death in the United States. Important steps for stroke survival include adequate public education, prehospital early recognition of stroke symptoms, and adequate emergency medical services with appropriate transport. Well-equipped stroke centers should be established and health care professionals such as anesthesiologists should be well-versed in the management of these patients. These patients may be encountered after rapid emergency department triage and often require urgent care and decision-making. Per the American Heart Association (AHA) Adult Basic Life Support (BLS) recommendations, the following key points must be considered in the management of strokes: • The presence and severity of a stroke should be rapidly assessed. The National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) is recommended by the AHA and may be encountered in the patient history during handover of care from the emergency department to the perioperative teams. • Laboratory studies may or may not be available. Only a blood glucose is needed prior to fibrinolytic administration per AHA guidelines. • Baseline electrocardiogram and troponins are recommended in patients presenting with acute ischemic stroke, however, this should not delay fibrinolytic therapy. Chest radiographs are noncontributory in this setting and should not delay fibrinolytic administration. • Brain imaging is critical to the timely evaluation of these patients. Radiologists should assess brain imaging findings including the size, location, vascular distribution of the infarction, as well as the presence of bleeding. • Administration of fibrinolytic therapy within the first few hours of onset of neurologic injury to improve outcome. The AHA suggests placing institutional protocols in place to facilitate the evaluation of a stroke and initiation of fibrinolytic treatment within 60 minutes of patient arrival. In taking a history of a patient with recent ischemic stroke, anesthesiologists should look for any fibrinolytic administration including the timing and signs of hemorrhagic conversion which can occur. • Supplemental oxygen to hypoxemic patients (SpO2 < 94%) should be provided since patients with acute stroke are at risk for respiratory compromise. Additionally, poor perfusion combined with hypoxemia will worsen ischemic brain injury. Respiratory compromise may occur due to partial airway obstruction, dysregulation of ventilation, aspiration, atelectasis, and pneumonia. Patients with decreased consciousness or bulbar dysfunction may have lost airway reflexes, and central periodic breathing (Cheyne-Stokes respiration) may be seen. Hyperoxia should also be avoided, thus titrate oxygen for a goal SpO2 < 100%. • Temperature regulation is key. These patients can present with hyperthermia soon after stroke onset. Hyperthermia is associated with poor neurologic outcome and should be addressed by treating the cause and monitoring temperature closely. • Extremes of systemic blood pressure in these patients can be detrimental and, in the absence of strong recommendations, values close to baseline blood pressure should be maintained, especially since these patients may have disturbed brain autoregulation. Pharmacologic interventions to lower as well as increase blood pressure should be available. • Fluid management goals should be to achieve euvolemia. These patients are often hypovolemic on presentation and this may lead to hypoperfusion and worsening of the brain injury. Conversely, hypervolemia may exacerbate brain edema due to ischemia and inflammation and may increase stress on the heart. • Glucose levels should be carefully monitored and kept within normal range. Hypoglycemia is rare and may lead to permanent brain damage. Conversely, hyperglycemia, which is more common in acute ischemic stroke due to stress, have been associated with worse clinical outcomes in multiple studies. • Close cardiac monitoring and continuous rhythm monitoring should be employed to screen for atrial fibrillation and other arrhythmias which are at highest risk of occurring during the first 24 hours since acute stroke onset. These patients present for endovascular intervention in the interventional radiology suite. Even if intra-arterial treatments are being considered, eligible patients should receive recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rTPA) therapy prior to arrival. Patient eligibility for rTPA is out of the scope of this question but can be found in the references below. The AHA's statements on endovascular interventions for the management of acute stroke include: • Similarly to intravenous fibrinolytic therapy, reduced time to reperfusion is associated with improved clinical outcomes • The usefulness of emergent intracranial angioplasty or stenting is not well-known
rationales:
Stroke patients frequently present with hyperthermia which can be detrimental for neurologic outcomes due to increased inflammation and metabolism. Patients should be maintained at normothermia.
Answer B: Overly aggressive reduction in glucose may lead to hypoglycemia and permanent neurological damage. It is appropriate to leave the current glucose level as is and recheck at a later interval. Per the American Heart Association, "Avoiding hypoglycemia was considered more important than the unproven benefits of treating moderate hyperglycemia."
Answer D: This hypertensive patient under stress and with a new stroke has risk factors for elevated blood pressure. She also may have an elevated baseline systemic blood pressure. It is appropriate to avoid extremes of blood pressure especially in stroke patients who may no longer have intact cerebral autoregulation. Extremes of blood pressure can be detrimental to neurologic outcomes.
bottomLine: Goals for patients presenting with acute stroke include normothermia, normotension, euvolemia, normal blood glucose levels, avoidance of hypoxemia (SpO2 < 94%), avoidance of hyperoxia (SpO2 100% on oxygen), and, most importantly, rapid fibrinolysis.

stem: What is the total arterial oxygen content in a patient with the following lab values? • Oxygen saturation: 100% • Hemoglobin: 10 g/dL • Arterial partial pressure of oxygen: 100 mm Hg
explanation: The total arterial blood oxygen content in a patient with a hemoglobin (Hb) of 10 g/dL, partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) of 100 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation (SaO2) of 100% would be 13.9 mL/dL. The total arterial blood oxygen content is 13.9 mL/dL = (10 g/dL × 1.36 mL O2/g Hb × 100%) + (100 mm Hg × 0.003 mL O2/dL blood/mm Hg). The total oxygen content in arterial blood is the sum of the oxygen bound to Hb and the amount of oxygen dissolved in the plasma. Each gram of normal Hb can bind ~1.36 mL of oxygen. Some texts reference 1.34 O2/g Hb because 1.36 is the carrying capacity under ideal conditions, and there are often small quantities of less effective forms of hemoglobin such as carboxyhemoglobin or methemoglobin in the blood. If all available sites of Hb are bound to oxygen, then the SaO2 will be 100%. Thus, the equation for the oxygen content bound to Hb is 1.36 mL O2/g Hb × Hb value of the patient × SaO2. The other source of oxygen is the amount dissolved in the plasma. According to Henry's law, the amount of dissolved oxygen is related to the partial pressure of oxygen and the solubility coefficient. The solubility coefficient of oxygen is 0.003 mL O2/dL/mm Hg, so the amount of oxygen dissolved in the plasma is 0.003 mL O2/dL/mm Hg × PaO2. By combining these 2 equations, the total oxygen content in arterial blood is (1.36 mL O2/g Hb × Hb value of the patient × SaO2) + (0.003 mL O2/dL/mm Hg × PaO2).
rationales:
The amount of oxygen dissolved in the plasma is 0.3 mL/dL. The PaO2 is 100 mm Hg, and the solubility coefficient of oxygen in blood is 0.003 mL O2/dL blood/mm Hg. Thus, 0.3 mL/dL = 100 mm Hg × 0.003 mL O2/dL blood/mm Hg.
Answer B: The amount of bound oxygen to Hb with an SaO2 of 100% is 13.6 mL/dL. Hemoglobin is 10 g/dL, SaO2 is 100%, and the Hb can carry 1.36 mL O2/g Hb. The amount of bound oxygen to Hb is 13.6 mL/dL = 10 g/dL × 1.36 mL O2/g Hb × 100%.
Answer D: The value of 20.7 mL/dL would be the total oxygen content in arterial blood for a healthy individual with an Hb of 15 g/dL, a PaO2 of 100 mm Hg, and an SaO2 of 100%. The total oxygen content in arterial blood is 20.4 mL/dL = (15 g/dL × 1.36 mL O2/g Hb x 100%) + (100 mm Hg × 0.003 mL O2/dL blood/mm Hg).
bottomLine: The total oxygen content in arterial blood is the sum of the oxygen bound to hemoglobin (Hb) and the amount of oxygen dissolved in the plasma. The total oxygen content in arterial blood can be calculated with the equation (1.36 mL O2/g Hb × Hb value of the patient × oxygen saturation) + (0.003 mL O2/dL/mm Hg × partial pressure of oxygen).
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. ""O2 content calculation"" Barash PG, et al. Clinical Anesthesia. Hemostasis and transfusion medicine. 8th ed. E-book. Page 432. Rosen IM, et al. Oxygen delivery and consumption. Uptodate. Literature review current through September 2021. This topic last updated April 13, 2021.

The total oxygen content in arterial blood is 20.4 mL/dL = (15 g/dL × 1.36 mL O2/g Hb x 100%) + (100 mm Hg × 0.003 mL O2/dL blood/mm Hg).
bottomLineHtml:
The total oxygen content in arterial blood is the sum of the oxygen bound to hemoglobin (Hb) and the amount of oxygen dissolved in the plasma.

The total oxygen content in arterial blood can be calculated with the equation (1.36 mL O2/g Hb × Hb value of the patient × oxygen saturation) + (0.003 mL O2/dL/mm Hg × partial pressure of oxygen).

stem: Which of the following regarding the blood-brain barrier is TRUE?

options.text: Fluid movement across the blood-brain barrier is dependent on hydrostatic pressure
options.html: Fluid movement across the blood-brain barrier is dependent on hydrostatic pressure

options.text: Mannitol readily crosses the blood-brain barrier
options.html: Mannitol readily crosses the blood-brain barrier

options.text: The blood-brain barrier facilitates the passage of hydrophilic substances
options.html: The blood-brain barrier facilitates the passage of hydrophilic substances

options.text: Water moves freely across the blood-brain barrier
options.html: Water moves freely across the blood-brain barrier

explanation: Water moves freely across the blood-brain barrier (BBB) based on the tonicity of intravascular fluid. The BBB forms a boundary between the central nervous system (CNS) and the rest of the body. It is a semipermeable membrane made up of the nearly fused junctions of vascular endothelial cells. The pores of this wall are lipophilic and small, thereby repelling hydrophilic molecules, such as charged ions, and large molecules. The relative osmolarity or oncotic pressure of the intravascular space determines the inward or outward flow of water across the BBB. The nature of the BBB is clinically relevant to the anesthesia provider for several reasons. The integrity of the BBB reflects neuroprotectivity. Disruption of the BBB, such as in cases of trauma or extreme hypertension, may lead to brain edema and CNS damage. While oncotic pressure generally drives the fluid gradient across a healthy BBB, hydrostatic pressure becomes the dominant factor once it is disrupted. The lipophilicity of the BBB also makes it a strategic drug target. Part of the reason volatile anesthetics induce general anesthesia is due to the lipid solubility of these gases across the BBB. Certain drugs with the same function may differ in CNS permeability because of the BBB, including the anticholinergic medication glycopyrrolate (does not cross BBB or cause sedation) and atropine (crosses the BBB and causes sedation).
rationales:
Fluid movement across the BBB is dependent on osmotic gradients. With the pathologic disruption of the BBB, hydrostatic pressure becomes more central to intracranial fluid movement.
Answer B: Mannitol is a sugar alcohol with osmotically active properties. It is given to promote diuresis during the oliguric phase of acute renal failure and in cases of elevated intraocular pressure and elevated intracranial pressure. Mannitol is also useful in flushing out harmful toxins. Its utility in elevated intracranial pressure stems from its large molecular weight, which makes it unable to penetrate the BBB. Mannitol then draws fluid from the brain into the intravascular space, which is then excreted as urine.
Answer C: The BBB is hydrophobic, which prevents the transit of ionized compounds. Its lipophilicity contributes to the penetration of volatile anesthetic into the CNS.
bottomLine: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) protects the central nervous system from pathogens and rapid fluctuations in its electrolyte fluid balance. Water moves freely across the BBB based on the tonicity of intravascular fluid. With the pathologic disruption of the BBB, hydrostatic pressure becomes more central to intracranial fluid movement.

stem: Which of the following will result in a leftward shift and increased slope of the carbon dioxide ventilatory response curve (i.e. a change from the black to the red curve)?

options.text: Increase of end-tidal oxygen concentration from 20% to 60%
options.html: Increase of end-tidal oxygen concentration from 20% to 60%

explanation: Surgical stimulus and heightened states of arousal (e.g. fear or anxiety) cause hyperventilation. This typically causes a leftward shift and increased slope of the carbon dioxide ventilatory response curve (VRC). A VRC illustrates how changes in a patient’s arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) will alter minute ventilation. The VRC is typically linear between PaCO2 values of 20-80 mmHg, such that increasing PaCO2 levels correspond to resultant increases in minute ventilation. Various factors can shift the PaCO2 baseline of a minute ventilation response. This baseline is illustrated as the PaCO2 at which a VRC intersects a ventilation curve (grey dotted line in these figures). The slope of the VRC represents the sensitivity of the ventilatory centers to elevated PaCO2. See the figure below for more details. MAC: minimum alveolar concentration.
rationales:
Volatile anesthetics at ≤1 MAC cause a rightward, parallel shift of the VRC. Volatile anesthetics >1 MAC reduce sensitivity to elevated PaCO2, cause a rightward shift, and reduce the slope of the VRC.
Answer C: Opioid, barbiturate, and other sedative-hypnotic medication administration shift the VRC to the right and depress the slope, in a dose-dependent manner. The result is a reduced minute ventilation and higher baseline PaCO2 therefore reducing minute ventilation.
Answer D: A change in end-tidal oxygen concentration from 20% to 60% will generally have no significant effect on a patient’s VRC. If the change represents correction of arterial hypoxemia, however, the curve may shift to the right with a decrease in the slope.
bottomLine: Factors that cause a leftward shift and an increased slope of a carbon dioxide ventilatory response curve include arterial hypoxemia, metabolic acidemia, surgical stimuli, and certain central nervous system pathologies. Factors that cause a rightward shift and a reduced slope of the curve include opioids, barbiturates, and sedative-hypnotic drugs. Volatile anesthetics ≤1 MAC cause a rightward, parallel shift of the VRC.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Co2-Vent Response Curve: Left Shift" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 7th edition, pp. 271-273.

stem: Which of the following occurs when adenosine triphosphate binds the myosin head during the muscle contraction cycle?

options.text: Myosin head binds the actin filament, forming a cross-bridge
options.html: Myosin head binds the actin filament, forming a cross-bridge

options.text: Myosin head decreases the angle, pulling itself along the actin filament
options.html: Myosin head decreases the angle, pulling itself along the actin filament

options.text: Myosin head releases from the actin filament
options.html: Myosin head releases from the actin filament

options.text: Myosin head returns to the cocked state, increasing the angle
options.html: Myosin head returns to the cocked state, increasing the angle

explanation: When adenosine triphosphate (ATP) binds the myosin head during the muscle contraction cycle, the myosin head detaches from the actin filament. Muscle contraction begins when the muscle cell is polarized when acetylcholine (ACh) binds to postsynaptic receptors. The depolarization spreads across the sarcolemma and into the t-tubules, activating the voltage-sensitive dihydropyridine receptors that are mechanically coupled to the ryanodine receptors in the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The ryanodine receptors release the stored Ca2+ into the sarcoplasm, increasing the intracellular Ca2+ concentration. The increased intracellular Ca2+ binds to troponin C on tropomyosin, leading to a conformational change such that the tropomyosin moves away, revealing a binding site on the actin filament for the myosin head to bind. The myosin head then binds the actin, forming a cross-bridge at a 90° angle. The myosin head releases a phosphate (Pi), and myosin pulls itself along the actin, decreasing the angle, causing the muscle to shorten and releasing the remaining adenosine diphosphate (ADP) molecule. Because the ATP binding site is now available, another ATP molecule binds to the site on the myosin head, releasing the myosin head from the actin filament. As the ATP is hydrolyzed on the detached myosin head, the myosin head returns to the cocked 90° angle state. The ADP and Pi remain on the myosin head. The myosin head is now ready to bind actin again. As long as the Ca2+ remains elevated, additional cross-bridging will occur, and muscle contraction ensues.
rationales:
When the level of Ca2+ is elevated, it binds to troponin C, leading to a conformational change such that the tropomyosin moves, revealing a binding site on the actin filament for the myosin head to bind. The myosin head then binds the actin, forming a cross-bridge at a 90° angle.
Answer B: The myosin head releases a Pi, and myosin pulls itself along the actin, decreasing the angle, causing the muscle to shorten, releasing the remaining ADP molecule.
Answer D: As the ATP is partially hydrolyzed on the detached myosin head, the myosin head returns to the cocked 90° angle state.
bottomLine: During the muscle contraction cycle, when adenine diphosphate is released from the myosin head, the adenine triphosphate (ATP) binding site is available to bind another molecule of ATP. When ATP binds the myosin head, it detaches from the actin filament.
trueLearnInsight: Mutations in the gene for the ryanodine receptor can result in the opening of the receptor after exposure to trigger agents such as volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine. This life-threatening condition is called malignant hyperthermia. This activation by triggering agents results in an uncontrolled release of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, leading to continued contraction of the muscles, causing increased oxygen consumption, carbon dioxide generation, and lactic acid production.

stem: Which of the following is an appropriate therapy for hypoxia secondary to negative pressure pulmonary edema (NPPE)?

options.text: Corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and edema
options.html: Corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and edema

explanation: The management of negative pressure pulmonary edema (NPPE) involves starting supplemental oxygen and positive endexpiratory pressure (PEEP), which can be via non-invasive methods or endotracheal intubation. Pulmonary edema following an airway obstruction can occur due to different mechanisms, but the predominant one involves creating a negative pressure in the presence of a closed glottis. This is an uncommon complication that occurs in about 0.1% of patients. When negative pressure is initiated while the glottis is closed or obstructed, a large intrapleural pressure is generated. The negative transpulmonary gradient favors the shifting of fluid from the pulmonary capillaries into the interstitium. The fluid accumulates so rapidly that the lymphatic system is unable to clear it. Situations that can create an occluded or obstructed glottis include laryngospasm, upper airway mass, or biting down on the endotracheal tube (simulates a closed glottis). These present with stridor, increased work of breathing (use of accessory muscles), paradoxical breathing (chest wall moves in with inspiration), and difficulty/inability to mask ventilate. The effects of negative pressure pulmonary edema are seen within 1-90 minutes. Hypoxia and diffuse interstitial/alveolar infiltrates on chest radiograph are noted, though radiographic findings may take time. Negative pressure pulmonary edema is self-limited, but it does prolong hospital stay. Management of negative pressure pulmonary edema involves improving respiratory function and avoiding further damage to the lungs. This includes supplemental oxygen and positive-pressure ventilation (non-invasive or endotracheal).
rationales:
Administering albuterol may help with bronchospasm or wheezing, however, in patients with negative pressure pulmonary edema the mainstay treatment involves supplemental oxygen and PEEP.
Answer B: Corticosteroids do not have a role in negative pressure pulmonary edema (also known as post-obstructive pulmonary edema).
Answer C: Diuretics are a possible option for NPPE, however, only after upper airway obstruction and hypoxemia are addressed. A bolus of furosemide is not likely to rapidly relieve hypoxemia, in comparison to PEEP.
bottomLine: Negative pressure pulmonary edema occurs in any setting where the patient has an occluded or obstructed airway and they then try to take a deep breath. The effects of the pulmonary edema (hypoxia, crackles on auscultation) can be noticed immediately or shortly after. Management involves supportive care with supplemental oxygen. Positive end-expiratory pressure can be useful and diuretics may be considered.

stem: Which of the following hormonal effects can be seen as a result of the surgical stress response?
explanation: Surgical stress, trauma, extensive burn injuries, and sepsis can lead to alterations in hormones, including an increase in adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) release. The nervous system activates the stress response after surgical stimuli through impulses sent from the operative site to the hypothalamus. Hypothalamic activation increases the activity of the sympathetic nervous system, which stimulates the adrenal medulla to secrete epinephrine and the pancreas to secrete glucagon. Hypothalamic activation also increases the output of the cardiovascular system and stimulates the release of corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH). The posterior pituitary gland is also stimulated during surgical stress, resulting in the release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). Plasma ADH concentrations are elevated after stresses, such as surgery, pneumonia, and myocardial infarction. The magnitude and duration of elevated ADH levels are proportional to the degree of stress. In septic shock, there is an initial increase in ADH concentrations, followed by a decrease to critically low concentrations. These extremely low concentrations are partially responsible for the persistent vasodilation in septic shock and hemodynamic instability after cardiac surgery. The release of CRH stimulates the anterior pituitary to release corticotropin (ACTH), which stimulates the adrenal glands to release cortisol. Cortisol mobilizes energy stores and promotes gluconeogenesis in the liver, leading to hyperglycemia. The serum concentration of catecholamines, norepinephrine, epinephrine, and dopamine increase after surgical stress. Additional stressors include anxiety, hypotension, hypothermia, burn injuries, and hypercarbia. In addition to their cardiovascular effects, catecholamines induce significant metabolic effects. Beta-2 adrenergic stimulation increases glycogenolysis, hepatic gluconeogenesis, and glucagon release while decreasing glycogen synthesis. Lipolysis is further increased by beta-2 adrenergic stimulation. The surgical stress response can also result in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. The pituitary gland is less responsive to gonadotropin-releasing hormone (Gn-RH), decreasing the release of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). Follicle-stimulating hormone and LH concentrations are minimally changed during surgery but decrease on the first postoperative day. The subsequent increase in CRH and cortisol levels contributes to the suppression of reproductive function. Testosterone concentrations significantly decrease in men after stress due to decreased production and increased clearance. Estrogen concentrations were shown to be decreased in premenopausal women during surgical stress, at times resulting in amenorrhea.
rationales:
Antidiuretic hormone is increased in response to surgical stress because it acts on V2 receptors in the kidney, leading to the insertion of aquaporin channels in the renal wall.
Answer B: Similarly to LH, FSH is decreased during the stress response.
Answer D: After surgical stimuli, the pituitary is less responsive to Gn-RH, resulting in the decreased release of LH and folliclestimulating hormone. This produces hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
bottomLine: The stress response to surgical stimuli can lead to various metabolic and physiologic alterations through impulses sent from the operative site to the hypothalamus. This response subsequently increases the activity of the sympathetic nervous system and the secretion of hormones from the anterior and posterior pituitary, most notably antidiuretic hormone, cortisol, and catecholamines. Reproductive hormones such as luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone decrease, resulting in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

The stress response to surgical stimuli can lead to various metabolic and physiologic alterations through impulses sent from the operative site to the hypothalamus.

This response subsequently increases the activity of the sympathetic nervous system and the secretion of hormones from the anterior and posterior pituitary, most notably antidiuretic hormone, cortisol, and catecholamines.

Reproductive hormones such as luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone decrease, resulting in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

stem: A patient undergoes valve-sparing aortic root replacement on hypothermic cardiopulmonary bypass. Which of the following changes would MOST LIKELY appear as the patient is cooled to 28°C?

options.text: Decreased arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide
options.html: Decreased arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide

options.text: Increased arterial partial pressure of oxygen
options.html: Increased arterial partial pressure of oxygen

options.text: Increased minimum alveolar concentration for isoflurane
options.html: Increased minimum alveolar concentration for isoflurane

explanation: The induction of hypothermia reduces the actual arterial partial pressures of dissolved gases such as carbon dioxide and oxygen. This occurs chiefly because the blood solubility of a gas increases with decreasing temperature. Arterial blood gas analysis has become a fundamental practice in perioperative and critical care settings because it facilitates the rapid assessment of several key metabolic parameters. Values obtained through direct gas analysis include the arterial pH, partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2), and PaO2. The arterial bicarbonate concentration can also be derived indirectly from these parameters. When they are considered together, these values provide a snapshot of the patient’s oxygenation, ventilation, and acid-base balance that may guide active clinical management. The PaCO2 is primarily a function of effective alveolar ventilation, the proportion of minute ventilation that participates in gas exchange. As alveolar ventilation increases, more carbon dioxide is released into the environment, and PaCO2 falls proportionally. By contrast, decreased alveolar ventilation, whether due to reduced total minute ventilation or increased dead space fraction, results in an increased PaCO2. However, several other factors also directly influence the PaCO2, including tissue-level metabolic rate as well as body temperature. Hypothermia is associated with a reduced PaCO2. This is because of the well-recognized connection between temperature and the solubility of gases in the blood. Gas solubility increases with decreasing temperature because a greater number of gas molecules shift into a dissolved (aqueous) phase and thus reduce the partial pressure of the gas “remaining” above the liquid solvent. When hypothermia is induced for therapeutic purposes—as is often performed during procedures requiring cardiopulmonary bypass or circulatory arrest—a patient will develop a relative respiratory alkalosis with reduced PaCO2 and increased arterial pH. For every 1°C reduction in core temperature, the patient’s PaCO2 can be expected to fall by ~2 mm Hg. During cardiopulmonary bypass, gas exchange is controlled by the bypass machine and can be manipulated by the perfusionist.
rationales:
Hypothermia is associated with a state of relative insulin resistance and reduced insulin release. This may produce significant hyperglycemia, requiring close glycemic monitoring and correction of elevated serum glucose concentrations with exogenous insulin administration.
Answer C: The effects of temperature on dissolved gases were described for CO2 in the question explanation, but these effects also apply to all dissolved gases, including oxygen. As the temperature falls, the blood solubility of oxygen also increases significantly, and PaO2 is reduced. With every 1°C decrease in core temperature, the patient’s PaO2 will fall by ~5 mm Hg.
Answer D: Because of slowed central nervous system activity and altered pharmacokinetics during hypothermia, lower doses of most anesthetics are required to maintain a state of general anesthesia. Using volatile anesthetics, such as isoflurane, notably results in substantially lower minimum alveolar concentrations for surgical anesthesia with significant temperature reductions. This trend correlates with the electroencephalographic changes produced by hypothermia itself. For instance, burst suppression without additional sedation may begin in patients cooled to 25°C, and electrical silence may be observed between 15°C and 20°C.
bottomLine: Hypothermia reduces both the arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide and the arterial partial pressure of oxygen because a decreased temperature causes an increase in gas solubility in the blood.
trueLearnInsight: Because arterial blood gas (ABG) is almost always interpreted at or near a physiologic body temperature (37°C), controversy persists regarding the question of whether ABG values should be corrected to the patient's actual body temperature during periods of hypothermia. Because a reduced PaCO2 predictably causes cerebral vasoconstriction, pH-stat management may better preserve cerebral blood flow and homogenous brain cooling, although this advantage comes at the expense of increased embolic risk.

stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE with regards to pulmonary oxygen toxicity of the neonate?

options.text: In most neonates, the fraction of inspired oxygen should be titrated to maintain oxygen saturation > 97% or a PaO2 > 150 mm Hg
options.html: In most neonates, the fraction of inspired oxygen should be titrated to maintain oxygen saturation > 97% or a PaO2 > 150 mm Hg

options.text: Respiratory burst of phagocytic cells by NADPH oxidase (NOX) reactions is a known source for reactive oxygen species formation
options.html: Respiratory burst of phagocytic cells by NADPH oxidase (NOX) reactions is a known source for reactive oxygen species formation

options.text: Significant hyperoxia primarily damages the liver, kidneys, and spleen
options.html: Significant hyperoxia primarily damages the liver, kidneys, and spleen

options.text: The rate of reactive oxygen species formation is directly correlated with cardiac output
options.html: The rate of reactive oxygen species formation is directly correlated with cardiac output

explanation: One of the important pathways in the development of reactive oxygen species (ROS) involves pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g. interferon-gamma, inflammatory protein 2). These cytokines lead to activation of NADPH oxidase (NOX) reactions in the electron transport chain of cellular mitochondria and lead to oxygen free radicals. Oxygen free radicals cause a variety of damage both at the microscopic and macroscopic level. Hyperoxia is defined as a state of excess supply of oxygen in tissues and organs that leads to ROS formation. After ROS form, tissue damage begins, most notably in the lung and the central nervous system. Exposure to 100% fractional inspired oxygen (FIO2) for as little as 4-6 hours has been shown to cause tracheobronchitis and decreased vital capacity. Critically ill patients and neonates have been shown to be deficient of anti-oxidant mechanisms and thus are more susceptible to oxygen toxicity. A devastating complication seen specifically to premature infants from high inspired oxygen concentrations is retinopathy, more specifically known as retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). Hyperoxia produces free radical oxygen species that cause vasoconstriction of the retinal vessels, which leads to scarring and possible retinal detachment. ROP may be mild and resolve spontaneously; however, more serious cases can lead to blindness. A systematic approach should be used when administering oxygen to every neonate: • Only use O2 when clinically indicated. Always start with a low amount of O2 (usually FiO2 of 0.3 or 0.4), and titrate to maintain oxygen saturation (SpO2) > 94% or to an arterial PaO2 > 100 mm Hg • Use protective lung volume ventilation strategies (i.e. tidal volumes 4-6 mL/kg) when able to, and consider using positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) to minimize further increases in FIO2 • Consider lower flows on the anesthesia circuit as high O2 flows can lead to desiccation of the airway (especially in neonates and young children) and increases the risk for lung barotrauma Two large randomized controlled trials studied FIO2 values and their effects on long-term chronic lung disease, duration of hospitalization, and neurodevelopmental measures in neonates. The Supplemental Therapeutic Oxygen for Pretheshold Retinopathy of Prematurity (STOP-ROP) trial concluded that there was no significant difference in the rate of progression to the threshold of ROP in the group of newborns cared for with lower O2 saturation range (89-94%) versus the higher group (96-99%). As a secondary outcome, the authors noticed an increased incidence of chronic lung disease and longer durations of hospitalizations, both which occurred at higher rates in the higher FIO2 group. In the Benefits of Oxygen Saturation Targeting (BOOST) trial, no differences were found in their primary outcomes, which were defined as growth and neurodevelopmental measures by 12 months corrected age. In the group who received higher O2 saturations (95-98%), these babies required oxygen for a longer period of time, had a higher dependence on oxygen at 36 weeks post-conceptual age, and needed home O2 therapy with higher frequencies compared to the infants in the lower O2 saturation group (91-94%).
rationales:
The goal when providing oxygen to a neonate is to start low and titrate FIO2 levels in order to maintain SpO2 levels > 94% or a PaO2 > 100 mm Hg. Hyperoxia can lead to unwanted complications including retinopathy.
Answer C: Hyperoxia and reactive oxygen species have been implicated in the pathophysiology of a variety of diseases, particularly chronic lung disease, central nervous system damage (i.e. retinopathy), and red blood cell damage.
Answer D: Metabolic conditions such as diabetes mellitus and increased FiO2 levels have been shown to increase the rate of reactive oxygen species formation, resulting in an imbalance between antioxidants and oxidants and damage to macromolecules such as nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids. Thus, the rate of reactive oxygen species formation is related to metabolic conditions and oxygenation, not cardiac output (if anything it would be indirectly linked to cardiac output).
bottomLine: Hyperoxia is defined as a state of excess supply of oxygen in tissues and organs. High fractional inspired concentrations of oxygen (FIO2) lead to formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). An important pathway involved in ROS formation is activation of NADPH oxidase (NOX) reactions in cellular mitochondria which cause cellular damage. Oxygen toxicity of the neonate usually manifests as chronic lung disease and central nervous system diseases (i.e. retinopathy of prematurity). When administering oxygen to a neonate, always start with the lowest possible amount of oxygen and titrate FIO2 levels to maintain SpO2 > 94% or PaO2 > 100 mg Hg.

stem: Which of the following CORRECTLY describes maternal oxygen consumption during the peripartum period?

options.text: Increased cardiac output during this period increases maternal oxygen consumption
options.html: Increased cardiac output during this period increases maternal oxygen consumption

options.text: Maternal respiratory alkalosis increases oxygen consumption
options.html: Maternal respiratory alkalosis increases oxygen consumption

options.text: One third of the increase in maternal oxygen consumption is accounted for by the combined metabolism of the fetus, placenta, and uterus
options.html: One third of the increase in maternal oxygen consumption is accounted for by the combined metabolism of the fetus, placenta, and uterus

options.text: Oxygen consumption returns to pre-pregnancy values by 48 hours postpartum
options.html: Oxygen consumption returns to pre-pregnancy values by 48 hours postpartum

explanation: Increased cardiac output during pregnancy increases maternal oxygen consumption. Overall, pregnancy increases oxygen consumption by 40-75% as a result of increased metabolic demand. In fact, two-thirds of this increase is attributed to fetal, placental, and uterine metabolism increase. Both at rest and during exercise, maternal oxygen uptake and consumption are increased in pregnant patients. The fetus, uterus, and placental tissues increase oxygen consumption at a higher rate than the mother per unit of weight. Each kilogram of maternal tissue consumes oxygen at a rate of approximately 4 mL/minute, while the fetoplacental unit consumes oxygen at a rate of approximately 12 mL/minute. During labor, oxygen consumption increases by up to 40% during the first stage and up to 75% during the second stage.
rationales:
The cause of maternal respiratory alkalosis is likely multifactorial, but mainly due to progesterone-induced central respiratory stimulation. Alkalosis leads to a left-shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, which would result in oxygen retention in the blood rather than release and consumption.
Answer C: Two-thirds of the increase in maternal oxygen consumption is accounted for by the combined metabolism of the fetus, placenta, and uterus.
Answer D: Functional residual capacity (FRC) increases after delivery, however, it remains below pre-pregnancy values for up to 1 to 2 weeks postpartum. Meanwhile, oxygen consumption, tidal volume, and minute ventilation remain elevated for up to 6 to 8 weeks postpartum.
bottomLine: Pregnancy increases oxygen consumption by 40-75% as a result of progressively increased tissue metabolism, especially that of the fetus, placenta, and uterus.

stem: A 56-year old man with a history of hypertension is undergoing video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) for a wedge resection of a suspicious pulmonary nodule. One-lung ventilation (OLV) is maintained using a double-lumen endotracheal tube, however, the patient readily becomes hypoxic despite confirmation of adequate tube placement. Which of the following oral antihypertensive agents is this patient MOST LIKELY taking?
explanation: ACE inhibitors are known to inhibit the process of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. During one-lung ventilation, this could potentially result in an increase in shunt flow through the non-ventilated lung and eventually cause systemic hypoxia. During one-lung ventilation, the physiologic process of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV) is able to decrease blood flow to the non-ventilated lung by around half, resulting in a decrease in shunt fraction through that lung and prevention of systemic hypoxemia. Decreases in alveolar oxygen concentration stimulate this response, which is primarily mediated by precapillary vasoconstriction. This local increase in pulmonary vascular resistance results in a preferential diversion of blood to areas of the lung that are adequately ventilated. This response will take around 2 hours to fully exert itself, however, the majority of the vasoconstriction will tend to occur in the first 20-30 minutes of local alveolar hypoxia. This is clinically relevant because acute hypoxia at the initiation of OLV could potentially take up to 20-30 minutes to reach the optimum effect of HPV. Thus, waiting and supporting the patient through a transient period of hypoxia may be necessary in order to allow surgery to proceed. There are many medications that have the effect of inhibiting HPV include vasodilators such as nitroglycerin, nitroprusside, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and calcium channel blockers. Even in patients who are not undergoing one-lung ventilation, these medications can induce clinically significant shunting that results in systemic hypoxia and could prompt their discontinuation. Physiologic states such as acidosis and hypercarbia will tend to induce pulmonary vasoconstriction, so it follows that alkalemia and hypocarbia act to inhibit hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, though the clinical effect of these states on HPV is of questionable significance. In addition to these physiologic states, any increase in pulmonary artery pressure will tend to increase the arteriovenous shunt fraction as the increased pulmonary pressures force blood through areas of the lung that would otherwise not receive perfusion. These states include pulmonary embolism, mitral stenosis, and potentially the use of certain vasopressors. It is important to note that pulmonary embolism primarily causes dead space ventilation through V/Q mismatching, but it also induces some degree of A/V shunting due to the increases in pulmonary artery pressures. It is traditionally taught that inhaled anesthetics are inhibitors of HPV. This teaching is however based on older studies utilizing enflurane and halothane, neither of which are in common use today. While the modern volatile anesthetics (isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane) are all indeed inhibitors of HPV, their actual effect is minimal and most anesthetics that involve the use of one-lung ventilation still utilize one of these agents for anesthetic maintenance. At 1 MAC, these agents will tend to inhibit HPV by about 20%. While this may seem like a large amount, this equates to only a 4% increase in the net shunt fraction during one-lung ventilation, a difference that is of questionable clinical significance. On another note, the HPV inhibitory effect of volatile anesthetics seems to be greater when the anesthetic is delivered to the alveolar capillaries via the alveolus itself and not the pulmonary circulation. Because the volatile anesthetic is not being delivered to the alveolus in the non-ventilated lung, the effect of volatile anesthetics on inhibiting HPV is mitigated. Because of these facts, there has been no evidence that the use of a totally intravenous anesthetic technique is beneficial for the sake of oxygenation than the use of a volatile anesthetic technique when performing surgery with one-lung ventilation. Answers A & C: Beta-blockers have not been shown to have a significant impact on hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction.
rationales: Thiazide diuretics have not been shown to have a significant impact on hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction.
bottomLine: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is an autoregulatory pulmonary reflex that causes precapillary vasoconstriction to preferentially divert the pulmonary circulation away from areas of alveolar hypoxia. All of the volatile anesthetics attenuate this reflex but to a mild and likely clinically insignificant degree. Propofol does not appear to have a significant effect on this reflex. Other vasodilating drugs such as nitroglycerin, nitroprusside, ACE-inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and calcium channel blockers all attenuate this reflex to varying degrees.
references: ABA Gaps In Knowledge Report, ITE 2016. "During one lung ventilation, ACE inhibitors can attenuate hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction." American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "HPV Inhibition: Drugs (B)" Miller's Anesthesia. Hypoxic Pulmonary Vasoconstriction in 8th Edition. Pages 1969 - 1970.
