Because of these facts, there has been no evidence that the use of a totally intravenous anesthetic technique is beneficial for the sake of oxygenation than the use of a volatile anesthetic technique when performing surgery with one-lung ventilation.

Answers A & C: Beta-blockers have not been shown to have a significant impact on hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction.
rationalesHtml: • Thiazide diuretics have not been shown to have a significant impact on hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction.
bottomLineHtml:
Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is an autoregulatory pulmonary reflex that causes precapillary vasoconstriction to preferentially divert the pulmonary circulation away from areas of alveolar hypoxia. All of the volatile anesthetics attenuate this reflex but to a mild and likely clinically insignificant degree.

Propofol does not appear to have a significant effect on this reflex. Other vasodilating drugs such as nitroglycerin, nitroprusside, ACE-inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and calcium channel blockers all attenuate this reflex to varying degrees.

stem: A 62-year-old man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis presents for the placement of a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt under general anesthesia. During the preprocedure evaluation, the patient appears sleepy and disoriented. Which of the following is the BEST explanation for why the presence of encephalopathy may be a relative contraindication to the procedure?
explanation: Hepatic encephalopathy is theorized to be due to hyperammonemia, which results from the accumulation of protein metabolism waste products. Therefore, procedures, such as a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS), that shunt blood away from the liver are likely to worsen hyperammonemia by reducing the hepatic conversion of ammonia to urea. Ammonia is the primary byproduct of protein metabolism. Protein metabolism occurs largely in the liver via deamination and transamination of amino acids. The liver is also responsible for a critical, final step in protein catabolism, the conversion of the relatively insoluble ammonia into the more water-soluble compound urea via the urea cycle which allows for renal excretion. Without sufficient conversion of ammonia to urea, hyperammonemia ensues, which is suspected to be a large contributor to the altered mental status associated with hepatic encephalopathy. For patients with liver disease, significant portal hypertension leads to a substantially increased risk of developing portosystemic collateral vessels and reversal of portal venous flow. This ultimately increases the risk of varices, ascites, and overt hepatic decompensation. Placing a low-resistance channel between the hepatic vein and the portal vein via the TIPS procedure can effectively offload the portal vein, reduce portal hypertension, and reduce the risk of developing these complications of portal hypertension. However, by diverting blood flow away from the portal vein, substances that require liver metabolism are also diverted away, including protein breakdown products such as ammonia. If ammonia is not delivered to the liver for conversion to urea, ammonia will accumulate, and hepatic encephalopathy may develop or worsen. Therefore, in a patient with signs of hyperammonemia such as hepatic encephalopathy, alternative treatments to first manage the hyperammonemia (ie, lactulose and rifaximin) may be more appropriate initially before the procedure.
rationales:
Recurrent esophageal varices are one of the indications for TIPS.
Answer B: Refractory ascites are an indication to perform TIPS. Reduction of portal hypertension and ascites after a TIPS procedure may improve hepatic function and reduce the risk of acute decompensation
Answer C: Patients with ascites related to end-stage liver disease are at an increased risk of aspiration; however, this is not a contraindication to the TIPS procedure or general anesthesia.
bottomLine: Ammonia is the primary byproduct of protein metabolism and must be converted to urea to be excreted. This occurs primarily in the liver, and therefore, shunting blood away from the liver is likely to worsen hyperammonemia by reducing the hepatic conversion of ammonia to urea. Therefore, hepatic encephalopathy is a relative contraindication to a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt procedure.

Ch. 16: Hepatic Physiology, Pathophysiology and Anesthetic Considerations. Section: Protein metabolism. 9th edition. Trefts E, et al. The liver. Curr Biol. 2017 Nov 6;27(21):R1147-R1151.

stem: Which of the following BEST describes the clinical difference between global and focal cerebral ischemia?

options.text: Focal ischemia can be tolerated for a longer period of time compared with global ischemia
options.html: Focal ischemia can be tolerated for a longer period of time compared with global ischemia

options.text: Focal ischemia will tend to result in neuronal depolarization, while global ischemia results in neurons left in their resting state
options.html: Focal ischemia will tend to result in neuronal depolarization, while global ischemia results in neurons left in their resting state

options.text: Global ischemia can cause EEG changes, while focal ischemia cannot
options.html: Global ischemia can cause EEG changes, while focal ischemia cannot

options.text: Global ischemia may be attenuated by hypothermia, while focal ischemia is not
options.html: Global ischemia may be attenuated by hypothermia, while focal ischemia is not

explanation: During focal ischemia, residual blood flow through collateral circulation results in a small but significant delivery of oxygen to the area of decreased flow downstream from the blood flow obstruction and allows for the generation of some adenosine triphosphate (ATP). The generation of a small amount of ATP helps to prevent catastrophic and irreversible membrane failure that would otherwise occur within minutes of the onset of ischemia. Clinically, therefore, focal ischemia appears to be more welltolerated compared with global ischemia. Cerebral ischemia results from impaired blood flow to the brain and is a common mechanism of acute brain injury. There are two types. Focal ischemia occurs when blood flow to restricted parts of the brain is insufficient, usually from thrombosis or embolism, and is confined to a specific region of the brain. Global ischemia typically results from systemic hypotension and encompasses wide areas of brain tissue. Compared to other organs, the brain has a very high rate of energy utilization. However, it has minimal energy storage capacity and is thus extremely vulnerable to a decrease in the blood flow that otherwise delivers a continuous supply of the oxygen and glucose required to create ATP. In a review of cerebral ischemia, the first focus must be on the critical cerebral blood flow thresholds that correspond to various levels of cerebral injury that occur if this blood flow is disrupted. Normal cerebral blood flow is approximately 50 mL/100 g/min, and a decrease in that flow will result in a gradual decline of cerebral function, eventually leading to catastrophic and irreversible membrane failure. When normal cerebral blood flow is 20 mL/100 g/min, the brain will begin to demonstrate electroencephalography (EEG) slowing, which corresponds to the dysfunction of the cortical neurons. When normal cerebral blood flow is 15 mL/100 g/min, the cortical EEG will be isoelectric. When normal cerebral blood flow is between 10 and 15 mL/ 100 g/min, there will be a gradual decrease in the energy supply that will eventually lead to neuronal death over the course of hours. When normal cerebral blood flow is between 6 and 10 mL/100 g/min, the neuronal injury will be temporarily reversible, but neuronal death will result if the flow is not rapidly restored. Neuronal injury and death can be attenuated through the slowing of the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen through the use of hypothermia and is how cases that use deep hypothermic circulatory arrest are possible without lasting cerebral injury. In focal ischemia, some residual collateral circulation to the area downstream of the blood flow obstruction will typically keep the neurons supplied with at least a small amount of oxygen and glucose. This allows focal ischemia to be much better tolerated compared to the global ischemia that occurs during circulatory arrest. The primary event that occurs during cerebral ischemia is the failure of ATP production due to decreased oxygen and glucose delivery to the neuron. This energy failure will result in rapid depolarization, the release of intracellular potassium into the extracellular space, an influx of both sodium and potassium, and the release of a very large amount of excitatory neurotransmitters, including glutamate. In both focal and global ischemia, activation of glutamate reactors will result in an increased influx of sodium and calcium that will eventually result in marked neuronal edema that occurs rapidly after neuronal depolarization.
rationales:
Neuronal ischemia, in general, will lead to depolarization and the influx of a large amount of extracellular sodium resulting in neuronal edema. This occurs in both focal and global ischemia.
Answer C: Both global and focal ischemia can induce changes in EEG, although focal ischemia will induce EEG changes only over the cortical area that is downstream to the area of blood flow obstruction. Focal slow-wave activity on EEG may be intermittent or persistent and is indicative of focal cerebral pathology of the underlying brain region; more persistent or consistently slower activity generally is indicative of more severe cerebral dysfunction. This intermittent or persistent focal slowing seen consistently over one head region or persistent, unvarying, and unreactive focal or generalized slow-wave activity is distinct from the generalized background slowing in the theta and delta frequencies, which is a normal finding on EEG during developmental slowing in children, adolescents, and some young adults or in the onset of drowsiness and sleep activity. Generalized background slowing indicates diffuse cerebral dysfunction, which, similarly to focal slowing, does not specify a cause.
Answer D: The neuronal injury in both global and focal ischemia is attenuated by decreasing the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen in the ischemic area through the use of therapeutic hypothermia.
bottomLine: Cerebral ischemia results from impaired blood flow to the brain and is a common mechanism of acute brain injury. There are two types. Focal ischemia occurs when blood flow to restricted parts of the brain is insufficient, usually from thrombosis or embolism, and is confined to a specific region of the brain. Global ischemia typically results from systemic hypotension and encompasses wide areas of brain tissue. Focal cerebral ischemia is more well-tolerated compared with global cerebral ischemia because of the preservation of some residual collateral flow to the ischemic region of the brain.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding total body water is TRUE?

options.text: Neonates have proportionally more extracellular fluid compared to adults
options.html: Neonates have proportionally more extracellular fluid compared to adults

options.text: Total body water comprises 80% of adult lean body mass
options.html: Total body water comprises 80% of adult lean body mass

options.text: Total body water is the sum of plasma volume and intracellular volume
options.html: Total body water is the sum of plasma volume and intracellular volume

options.text: Total body water proportion (%) increases in obesity
options.html: Total body water proportion (%) increases in obesity

explanation: Neonatal interstitial fluid is proportionally three times larger than in adults contributing to a proportionally larger extracellular fluid volume. In a healthy human adult, total body water (TBW) comprises approximately 55-60% of lean body mass in men and 45-50% in women. Although most body tissue is 70-80% water, this is offset by bone (20% water) and fat (10-15% water). TBW is made up of 1/3 extracellular fluid and 2/3 intracellular fluid. Extracellular fluid volume is further subdivided into 3/4 interstitial fluid and 1/4 plasma fluid. Meanwhile, in neonates, TBW is 70-80% with a greater proportion of extracellular fluid compared to adults. In fact, premature babies have an extracellular fluid compartment that exceeds intracellular fluid volume. The proportionally greater volume of distribution warrants higher doses per kilogram compared to older children and adults. TBW percentage decreases up until around age 12 where it normalizes at adult values. This percentage then begins to decrease again with aging due to an increase in fat content although TBW volume remains the same. The proportionally reduced distribution for hydrophilic drugs leads to greater plasma concentrations. Conversely, these physiologic changes lead to a decrease in the plasma concentration of lipophilic drugs. % TBW by age Age TBW (%) Table adapted from Miller's Anesthesia, 9th Edition
rationales:
Total body water comprises 70-80% of lean body mass in neonates as opposed to ~60% in adults.
Answer C: Total body water is the sum of extracellular volume and intracellular volume. The extracellular volume consists of interstitial fluid and plasma fluid volumes.
Answer D: The proportion of total body water (% water per kg body mass) is significantly lower than lean individuals because adipose tissue contains much less water compared to other tissues.
bottomLine: Total body water (TBW) is an important factor in assessing a patient's fluid status, assessing fluid requirements, and in the context of administering anesthetic drugs. The % TBW is highest as a neonate, normalizes by teenage years, and decreases again in old age. Men have a higher % TBW (~60%) compared to women (~50%) and obese individuals have lower % TBW than lean individuals due to the low amount of water in adipose tissue.

stem: What property of the kidneys allows for increased efficiency in the elimination of drugs from systemic circulation?

options.text: Active protein transporters in proximal renal tubules
options.html: Active protein transporters in proximal renal tubules

options.text: Catalyzing reduction-oxidation reactions to produce byproducts for elimination
options.html: Catalyzing reduction-oxidation reactions to produce byproducts for elimination

options.text: Ionization of drugs within the medulla
options.html: Ionization of drugs within the medulla

options.text: Lipid-mediated free diffusion of drugs < 400 Dalton
options.html: Lipid-mediated free diffusion of drugs < 400 Dalton

explanation: The kidney is able to reabsorb and excrete numerous compounds. The chemical structure, delivery of metabolites, and available transport proteins contribute to the overall function of the renal system. The kidney is able to excrete unchanged hydrophilic molecules as well as metabolites from hepatic breakdown via Phase I and Phase II reactions (recall Phase I is reductionoxidation reactions and Phase II is conjugation). Should the kidney have been designed to excrete in a passive manner, simply dependent on drug delivery via blood flow, there would be complete inefficiency in drug excretion. Located in the proximal renal tubules are active protein transporters or organic acids and bases that allow for the elimination of the metabolites. This allows for the kidneys to filter and excrete metabolites more efficiently despite receiving a large cardiac output. Nevertheless, this system is still subject to dysfunction due to factors such as decreased cardiac output and intrinsic renal disease that allow for metabolites to increase in concentration.
rationales:
This form of reaction is done in the liver. Recall Phase I is reduction-oxidation reactions and Phase II is conjugation.
Answer C: Drug ionization does lead to decreased elimination and its mechanism is unrelated to increasing efficiency.
Answer D: This is the mechanism by which some drugs cross the blood-brain barrier.
bottomLine: Renal disease can lead to an increase in drug metabolites. It is the kidney’s active protein transporters in the proximal renal tubules that increase the efficiency with which these drugs are eliminated.
trueLearnInsight: Common anesthetic drugs that are associated with significant renal excretion include aminoglycosides, cephalosporins, digoxin, neostigmine, rocuronium, and sugammadex.
references: ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. “Renal Physiology: Drug Excretion" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 7th edition. Page 161

stem: Which of the following lung volumes or parameters in the neonate is comparable to that of an adult (per mL/kg)?
explanation: Tidal volumes in the neonate are similar to the adult on a volume per kg basis. They have increased respiratory rates which thereby increases the neonate's minute ventilation as compared to the adult. The neonate's closing volume is higher and can approach their normal tidal volume which can result in premature closure of small airways. The neonate has a higher minute ventilation due to their higher oxygen consumption. With a similar functional residual capacity compared to the adult but a higher minute ventilation, the neonate's ratio of minute ventilation to FRC is two to three times higher. This leads to a decreased oxygen reserve but a faster inhalation induction in the neonate.
rationales:
Closing volumes are high in the neonate and may be near the normal tidal volume.
Answer B: While the tidal volume is comparable to the adult on an mL/kg basis, the neonate's respiratory rate is increased, therefore increasing their minute ventilation as well.
Answer C: The neonate's respiratory rate is increased as compared to the adult.
bottomLine: Tidal volume in the neonate is comparable to an adult on a volume/kg basis while their closing volume, respiratory rate, and minute ventilation are increased.
references: Barash Anesthesia. Neonatal Anesthesia in Seventh Edition. Page 1181. ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Neonatal Physiology: Lung Volumes Vs Adult"

stem: A 25-year-old man contains 50 L of total body water. How much fluid is contained intravascularly?
explanation: The extracellular fluid compartment (ECF) is one-third of the total body water. The intravascular compartment is one-fourth of the ECF. Thus, the intravascular fluid compartment is 1/4 × 1/3 = 1/12 ≈ 8% of total body water. If total body water is 50 L, then the amount contained intravascularly is 4 L (50 L × 8%). Total body water (percentage of total body water) is divided into extracellular (33%) and intracellular (ICF; 67%) fluid compartments, and each is further subdivided into smaller compartments. The ECF comprises interstitial (25%) and intravascular (5%) compartments. The interstitial fluid compartment is the fluid around cells and outside the vasculature. The intravascular fluid compartment is bound by the vascular endothelium, which allows for the free passage of small ions into the interstitium. Although small ions may pass into the interstitium freely, the tight junctions between the endothelial cells prevent the movement of larger molecules such as albumin. As a result, these proteins are osmotically active and capable of drawing in water intravascularly. The composition of total body water
rationales:
The interstitial fluid compartment is 25% of the total body water, 12.5 L for the patient described in this question.
Answer C: The ECF is 33% of the total body water, 16.6 L for the patient described in this question.
Answer D: The ICF is 67% of the total body water, 33.3 L for the patient described in this question.
bottomLine: The intravascular fluid compartment is 8% of total body water.
trueLearnInsight: Colloid solutions tend to remain intravascularly for a longer duration than crystalloids and have equal efficacy in fluid resuscitation when given in proper amounts. Colloids are typically indicated in fluid resuscitation in severely intravascularly depleted patients such as those with hemorrhagic shock (while awaiting the transfer of blood) or severe hypoalbuminemia or burn patients. Notably, colloid solutions such as albumin are prepared in normal saline; thus, they have a chloride concentration between 145 and 154 mEq/L. Colloids such as dextrans are limited by side effects, such as a reduction in blood viscosity, platelet adhesion, red blood cell aggregation, and von Willebrand factor levels. Due to their side effects, dextrans can improve blood flow and reduce thrombus formation.

stem: In which of the following clinical scenarios is the use of anesthetic agents to induce pharmacologic burst suppression MOST appropriate?

options.text: Aortic root surgery with cerebral flow disruption
options.html: Aortic root surgery with cerebral flow disruption

explanation: The induction of a pharmacologic burst suppression utilizing anesthetic agents has been shown to improve mortality in patients with status epilepticus that is refractory to all other abortive therapies. Pharmacologic burst suppression is an electroencephalographic (EEG) finding where the EEG will display a rhythmic alternation between prolonged periods of flat-line EEG alternating with a short period of with bursts of electrical activity. The practice of inducing this electroencephalographic state is controversial due to limited evidence that demonstrates benefit in only a select few clinical scenarios. The theory behind burst suppression is that by inducing a largely electrically quiet brain state, the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2) can be decreased by up to 50%. This is preferable to an entirely silent EEG as the presence of brief periods of activity allow for monitoring of the depth of anesthesia. By allowing for brief bursts of electrical activity, the provider is able to ensure that they are not providing an excessive amount of anesthetic agent to achieve a largely flat EEG. If it were entirely quiet, there would be no way to know just how much extra agent was being administered to ensure this EEG state, and emergence from the pharmacologic coma would be difficult to accurately predict. No specific guidelines exist as to the optimal ratio of burst to suppression on an EEG in this state, and many providers utilize a goal of 1:10 burst to suppression when targeting this EEG state though this is a largely arbitrary value. In theory, periods of decreased cerebral perfusion might benefit from a pharmacologically decreased CMRO2, however, this has not been largely borne out in practice. For instance, no benefit has been shown in surgeries for cerebral aneurysms nor in patients recovering following a cardiac arrest. In cases where the electrical activity of the brain is unable to be controlled, such as in refractory status epilepticus, there does exist some benefit for the pharmacologic induction of a burst suppression EEG, and there may also be some benefit both in traumatic brain injury and in carotid endarterectomies when shunting is not performed. Agents that are typically used to induce burst suppression include propofol, halogenated anesthetics (typically isoflurane), or barbiturates. Clinically, the amount of barbiturate that is needed to induce burst suppression will result is an extremely protracted emergence from the anesthetic over the course of days. Propofol and the halogenated anesthetics allow for a much more titratable EEG and more rapid emergence. Severe hypothermia will eventually induce burst suppression and eventual EEG silence, though the temperature at which this occurs is variable in patients and insufficient evidence exists as to whether targeting this EEG finding should be the goal of deep hypothermic circulatory arrest in patients undergoing surgeries requiring this level of cerebral blood flow disruption.
rationales: Insufficient evidence exists to determine if there is a benefit to targeting an EEG with burst suppression during surgeries that involve cerebral flow disruption (e.g. deep hypothermic circulatory arrest). Answers B & C: Pharmacologic burst suppression has been shown to not improve outcomes in patients undergoing cerebral aneurysm surgeries or following a cardiac arrest.
bottomLine: Pharmacologic burst suppression is an EEG finding induced by anesthetic agents which displays long periods of electrical silence punctuated by brief bursts of electrical activity. In this state, the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen decreases by up to 50%, and it may be protective in pathologic states of poor cerebral perfusion though this is controversial. Anesthetic agents that are utilized to induce burst suppression include propofol, halogenated anesthetic gasses, and barbiturates. Burst suppression is typically avoided in most anesthetic settings but has been shown to improve mortality in status epilepticus.

stem: Which of the following is a TRUE statement regarding respiratory surfactant in the neonate?

options.text: Decreased surfactant is not directly associated with respiratory distress syndrome
options.html: Decreased surfactant is not directly associated with respiratory distress syndrome

options.text: Decreased surfactant reduces work of breathing and increases lung compliance
options.html: Decreased surfactant reduces work of breathing and increases lung compliance

options.text: Exogenous surfactant should not be given through an endotracheal tube
options.html: Exogenous surfactant should not be given through an endotracheal tube

options.text: Surfactant acts to maintain the functional residual capacity at exhalation
options.html: Surfactant acts to maintain the functional residual capacity at exhalation

explanation: Surfactant plays an indispensable role in the pulmonary development of the neonate. It acts to expand alveoli and maintain the functional residual capacity at exhalation. Preterm neonates who are deficient in surfactant are at risk of respiratory distress syndrome which can result in atelectasis, hypoxia, decreased lung compliance, and an increase in the work of breathing. Exogenous surfactant should be utilized as both prophylaxis and treatment for respiratory distress syndrome. It can be administered through an endotracheal tube and can be used to improve gas exchange in neonates with heart failure, sepsis, or other systemic illness.
rationales:
Decreased surfactant has been associated with respiratory distress syndrome in the neonate.
Answer B: A decrease in surfactant causes atelectasis with subsequently decreased lung compliance and an increased work of breathing.
Answer C: Exogenous surfactant can be given through an endotracheal tube for both prophylaxis and treatment of respiratory distress syndrome.
bottomLine: Surfactant plays an important role in preventing atelectasis and increasing lung compliance while decreasing the work of breathing. It acts to maintain the functional residual capacity at exhalation and can be given through the endotracheal tube to prevent or treat respiratory distress syndrome in the neonate.
references: Barash Anesthesia. Neonatal Anesthesia in Seventh Edition. Page 1182. ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Neonatal Physiology: Respiratory Surfactant"

stem: Which of the following endocrine abnormalities is MOST LIKELY to be associated with difficult airway management?
explanation: Growth hormone-secreting tumors result in acromegaly and are most likely to be associated with difficult airway management. Acromegaly occurs as a result of excess growth hormone. This leads to a number of anatomic and physiologic effects, many of which are relevant to the practice of anesthesia. The excess growth hormone causes enlarged connective tissue, bones, and visceral organs. This includes macrognathia (enlarged jaw), macroglossia (enlarged tongue), as well as enlargement of the nose, epiglottis, pharyngeal tissue, and laryngeal tissue. Due to the soft tissue enlargement, many patients with acromegaly have obstructive sleep apnea and it is also common to have a component of central sleep apnea. Patients may also experience subglottic stenosis. All of these factors can impact the ability of a provider to adequately mask ventilate and intubate. The literature supports a rate of difficult intubation ranging from 2-5% in large population studies of patients without acromegaly. While the literature on patients with acromegaly is limited, there is at least one prospective trial and several retrospective publications describing difficulties with intubation of acromegalic patients, with an incidence of difficult intubation in 10-30% of patients. Successful intubation of acromegalic patients in these studies was aided by the use of external laryngeal pressure and gum elastic bougies (tracheal tube introducers). As with any patient, a thorough airway exam should be performed including assessment of Mallampati score, neck mobility, and jaw mobility. Alternatives to direct laryngoscopy such as awake fiberoptic intubation should be considered for these patients, especially if providers have had prior difficulty with intubation.
rationales:
Acute pituitary deficiency in the perioperative setting is associated with hypotension. This is not known to be associated with difficult airway management.
Answer B: Adrenocorticotropic hormone-secreting tumors in the anterior pituitary cause the condition of glucocorticoid excess known as Cushing’s disease. While these patients often have obesity and obstructive sleep apnea, their anatomy does not pose the same difficulties in airway management as the patient with acromegaly.
Answer D: Syndrome of inappropriate anti-diuretic hormone (SIADH) is a condition in which the body produces too much antidiuretic hormone. This results in hyponatremia and reduced serum osmolarity. SIADH is not known to be associated with difficult airway management.
bottomLine: Patients with acromegaly are at increased risk of difficult airway management due to enlargement and distortion of tissues in the face, oropharynx, and larynx. Thorough airway assessment should be performed preoperatively and providers should have a low threshold for using techniques such as awake fiberoptic intubation to secure the airway.

stem: A 70-year-old 80 kg male undergoes exploratory laparotomy for a perforated duodenum and is now in the ICU intubated on a FiO2 of 50%, PEEP of 5 cmH2O, respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute, and tidal volume of 480 milliliters. His SpO2 is 80%, blood pressure is 100/50 mm Hg, pulse is 80 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.2 degrees Celsius. An arterial blood gas is drawn with the following results: pH: 7.30 PaO2: 55 mm Hg PaCO2: 52 mm Hg HCO3: 18 mEq/L A chest radiograph shows bilateral fluffy infiltrates. A pulmonary artery catheter is inserted with a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 10 mm Hg. Which of the following interventions is LEAST LIKELY to improve the patient's PaO2?
explanation: This patient likely has Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) with resultant hypoxemia from shunting. Increasing FiO2 is the least likely intervention to improve the patient's PaO2. ARDS is highly prevalent in the ICU population and accounts for 10-15% of all ICU admissions. ARDS can arise from direct lung injury (ie pneumonia) or in association with extrapulmonary infection (sepsis) and is characterized by inflammatory infiltration of the lung resulting in diffuse alveolar damage. This pulmonary edema and alveolar collapse can result in severe ventilationperfusion mismatch (low V/Q ratio aka shunt). The Berlin Definition of ARDS (see table below) characterizes the severity of disease based on the degree of hypoxemia. Treatment of ARDS is largely supportive and includes treatment of inciting events, avoidance of complications, and mechanical ventilation. Mechanical ventilation strategies are primarily directed towards optimizing gas exchange while minimizing additional lung injury (lung-protective ventilation with tidal volumes of 4-6 mL/kg and plateau pressure < 30 mm Hg). Lung recruitment strategies are often utilized and include increasing PEEP, recruitment maneuvers, and prone positioning. These methods help improve FRC and maintain the patency of available alveolar units for gas exchange. Because ARDS is characterized by significant intrapulmonary shunting, the hypoxemia is relatively unresponsive to oxygen therapy and therefore increasing the FiO2 is unlikely to improve gas exchange. Berlin Definition of ARDS Timing Within 1 week of known clinical insult OR new/worsening respiratory symptoms Imaging* Bilateral opacities - not fully explained by effusions, lobar/lung collapse, or nodules Origin of Edema Not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload** Oxygenation (with PEEP or CPAP ≥5 mmHg) Mild: PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 201-300 mm Hg Moderate:PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 101-200 mmHg Severe: PaO2/FiO2 ratio ≤100 mmHg *via chest radiography or CT scan **often requires objective assessment (eg echocardiography)
rationales:
Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) would bypass the diseased lungs and provide mechanical support of gas exchange thus improving PaO2. The use of ECMO to support patients with severe ARDS became prominent during the influenza pandemic of 2009. A multicenter randomized control trial demonstrated that patients randomized to ECMO consideration had increased likelihood of disability-free survival at 6 months. However, widespread use of this treatment option is limited by its invasive nature, cost, and the need for specialized treatment centers.
Answer C: PEEP helps to improve FRC and maintain the patency of available alveolar units for gas exchange. Improved gas exchange (ie less V/Q mismatch) would improve PaO2.
Answer D: Prone positioning for treatment of ARDS has been rigorously studied. Justification for this method centers around the idea that there is A) less alveolar collapse due to gravity and B) more even distribution of perfusion in the prone position as compared to the supine position. A 2010 meta-analysis of seven RCTs found a mortality benefit to prone positioning in patients with a severe ARDS (ie PaO2/FiO2 ratio of ≤100). However, because this treatment method is associated with additional complications (endotracheal tube dislodgement, pressure ulcers, etc.), it is often used as a rescue therapy when conventional ventilation strategies have failed.
bottomLine: Oxygen therapy is of limited value with large intrapulmonary shunts due to limitation of gas exchange and requires alternative therapies to improve V/Q matching.

stem: While on rounds in the ICU, a patient is presented who has hypoxemia and hypercarbia. The patient in question has an oxygen saturation of 86% on room air with an increased alveolar-arterial gradient. Which of the following would be MOST likely?
explanation: Atelectasis (A) is associated with an increased alveolar arterial (Aa) gradient. The alveolar arterial oxygen gradient is a calculation used to help determine ventilation-perfusion abnormalities. The equation compares the relationship between alveolar oxygen tension and arterial blood oxygen level. When the gradient is increased, a V/Q mismatch or diffusion problem is occurring. A normal Aa gradient occurs in hypoventilation and when the FIO2 is decreased. A normal A-a gradient is 5 - 10 mm Hg for a young adult nonsmoker. The A-a gradient increases about 1 mm Hg per decade of life, so a 40-year-old would have a normal A-a gradient of < 14 mm Hg. A conservative estimate of A-a gradient can be calculated with the same equation as pediatric endotracheal tube size: (Age / 4) + 4. A-a gradient is then A-a = PA – PaO2 Atelectasis is the collapse of alveoli which results in shunting of blood. Atelectasis can be caused by compression due to increased abdominal pressure or increased closing capacity. Atelectasis can also occur from loss of surfactant, which increases alveolar collapse as a result of increased surface tension across the alveoli. Additionally, absorption atelectasis occurs from diffusion of all gas from out of the alveoli and into the blood. Critical illness myopathy (B) is a syndrome of global muscle weakness and destruction that develops in some critically ill patients. These patients have severe muscle weakness and hypoventilate as a result. Hypoventilation does not cause an increase in the Aa gradient. Myasthenia gravis (C) is an autoimmune disease in which antibodies to acetylcholine receptors are produced. Myasthenia gravis causes a progressive weakness which leads to hypoventilation. An opioid overdose (D) causes central hypoventilation because of a right shift and down slope of the CO2 response curve. Treatment for an opioid overdose primarily involves support of ventilation. Pickwickian syndrome (E) is also known as obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Patients with Pickwickian syndrome hypoventilate at night and become hypercarbic and hypoxic. Many patients with Pickwickian syndrome also have obstructive sleep apnea, but Pickwickian syndrome is a central form of hypoventilation. As stated earlier hypoventilation does not affect the Aa gradient because gas diffusion in the lungs is not significantly changed. Pickwickian syndrome is associated with right-sided congestive heart failure and pulmonary hypertension from hypoxia.
bottomLine: The A-a gradient is increased (> 15 mm Hg) with shunting, dead space ventilation, and diffusion defects. The A-a gradient is not increased (5 - 10 mm Hg) with hypoventilation or low FiO2 in isolation.
references: Miller, Ronald D. Miller’s Anesthesia. 7th edition. 2010. Marino, Paul L. The ICU Book. 3rd edition. 2006. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "High A-a gradient: Causes"

stem: Which of the following is the single best choice in providing an assessment of hepatic protein synthesis?
explanation: Coagulation factors are the single best measure to provide an assessment of hepatic protein synthesis function. This is because clotting factors have a short half-life. For example, factor VII has a half-life of only four to six hours – this is compared to albumin which has a half-life of approximately 21 days. Because approximately 20 to 30 percent of normal coagulation activity is necessary for appropriate coagulation, coagulation dysfunction tests suggest severe liver dysfunction. An excellent indicator of such dysfunction is measurements of prothrombin time. Nevertheless, prothrombin times may be high because of vitamin K deficiency, disseminated intravascular coagulation, congenital clotting factor deficiencies, and certain drugs.
rationales:
Evaluation of protein synthesis by the liver can be determined by evaluating the serum levels of proteins synthesized by the liver. In this respect, serum albumin levels can make assessments of the liver protein synthetic capacity. Serum albumin is synthesized by hepatocytes, but because it has a half-life of 21 days in the serum, its correlation to the protein synthetic function of the liver should be assessed over several weeks. However, hypoalbuminemia is not a reliable indicator of hepatic synthetic function because it can occur with protein-losing enteropathies, increased vascular permeability, fluid retention, nephrotic syndrome, chronic infections, increased catabolism, and malnutrition. Thus, it has a long half-life. Additionally, acute hepatic dysfunction will only affect albumin levels mildly.
Answer C: Serum Gamma-Glutamyl transferase (GGT) is an enzyme that is found in hepatic as well as other tissues. GGT is the most sensitive indicator of biliary tract disease, but because it is found in other tissues as well it is not as useful as 5’NT measurements to determine if an elevated alkaline phosphatase is due to liver damage. Nevertheless, the evaluation of GGT is not better than the evaluation of coagulation factors in determining the function of hepatic protein synthesis.
bottomLine: Hepatic protein synthesis is best assessed by measuring coagulation factors.

stem: Which of the following neurotransmitters is used by the both the parasympathetic and sympathetic nervous system to transmit a signal at the ganglia?
explanation: Acetylcholine is used by both the parasympathetic and sympathetic nervous systems at the ganglia to transmit signals from the preganglionic to the postganglionic neurons. The parasympathetic nervous system uses acetylcholine at the postganglionic neurons and the target organ to produce an effect. The sympathetic system utilizes primarily norepinephrine. The autonomic nervous system is composed of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems. The sympathetic nervous system lies within the lateral gray column of the spinal cord where its cells bodies are located spanning from T1-L2. The nerves housed within the spinal cord that then synapse at the ganglia are the preganglionic neurons. They then activate postganglionic neurons by releasing acetylcholine. The postganglionic neurons then release norepinephrine at most target sites to activate the adrenergic receptors with the exception of epinephrine at the adrenal medulla and acetylcholine at sweat glands. The parasympathetic nervous system contains a cranial and pelvic portion. The cranial portion consists of cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X, and the pelvic portion consists of the pelvic splanchnic nerves from S2-4. The parasympathetic neurons are similar to the sympathetic neurons as they both utilize acetylcholine at the ganglia to transmit the signal. Parasympathetic neurons release acetylcholine at their target organs to produce an effect. A difference between the two systems is that the parasympathetic preganglionic neurons synapse on the ganglia close to the organs they innervate resulting in short postganglionic neurons.
rationales:
Epinephrine is used by the postganglionic cells of the sympathetic nervous system at the adrenal medulla.
Answer C: Glycine is not used by either system but is an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain and spinal cord.
Answer D: Norepinephrine is used by the postganglionic cells of the sympathetic nervous system to produce an effect at the target sites.
bottomLine: Acetylcholine is utilized by both the parasympathetic and sympathetic nervous system to transmit signals from preganglionic to postganglionic neurons.

stem: A 54-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a lower gastrointestinal bleed. The patient’s blood pressure is 82/51 mm Hg. What is the mechanism of action for renin in this patient?

options.text: Causes the release of aldosterone from the adrenal medulla
options.html: Causes the release of aldosterone from the adrenal medulla

options.text: Converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II
options.html: Converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II

options.text: Decrease renal excretion of sodium and water
options.html: Decrease renal excretion of sodium and water

explanation: Renin is released from the kidneys in response to a decrease in blood pressure. It cleaves the peptide angiotensinogen to create angiotensin I (C). Renin is created and stored by the cells in the afferent arterioles of the kidney. Renin secretion can be caused by 3 different mechanisms: a decrease in serum NaCl concentration sensed by the kidneys, a decrease in blood pressure sensed by kidney baroreceptors, or activation of renal B1 receptors by norepinephrine. Decreases in blood pressure, such as that displayed by the patient above, would cause a release of renin into the serum by at least one of these mechanisms. Renin then acts by cleaving the peptide angiotensinogen to create angiotensin I. Angiotensin I is then converted to angiotensin II by angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE). Angiotensin II (Ang II) has several effects, which combine to increase systemic perfusion in patients. The most immediate response to Ang II is an increase in blood pressure caused by an increase in systemic vascular resistance. Ang II activates the angiotensin1 (AT1) receptors on vascular smooth muscle cells, causing constriction of the arterioles. Ang II also augments the sympathetic nervous system by inhibiting norepinephrine reuptake into nerve terminals. It also stimulates the release of catecholamines from the adrenal medulla. In addition, Ang II causes a centrally mediated increased thirst and enhances the release of vasopressin. These effects are almost immediate, but are not long-lasting. Ang II also has longer lasting effects in the body. In addition to its effects on blood pressure, it stimulates remodeling of the cardiovascular system, causing hypertrophy of cardiac cells and increased collagen deposition. It also has profound effects on the kidney, causing a decrease in the urinary excretion of both sodium and water. Lastly, Ang II stimulates the adrenal cortex to synthesize and release aldosterone. Aldosterone also acts on the kidneys to decrease the urinary excretion of sodium and water. This ultimately leads to an increase in blood volume and therefore blood pressure.
rationales:
Angiotensin II leads to the increased release of aldosterone. Angiotensin II also increases blood pressure by direct vasoconstriction.
Answer B: Angiotensin I is converted to angiotensin II by angiotensin converting enzyme.
Answer D: Both angiotensin II and aldosterone act on the kidneys to decrease the urinary excretion of sodium and water.
bottomLine: A decrease in blood pressure stimulates the release of renin into the serum from the renal tubules. Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which is then converted to angiotensin II by ACE. Angiotensin II causes an increase in blood pressure by direct vasoconstriction, enhancing the sympathetic nervous system, and causing an increase of aldosterone.
references: Brunton, LL. et. al. Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 12th edition, Chapter 26 American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Hypovolemia: Renin-angiotensin Response"

stem: What is the reflexive efferent output that results from the stretching of aortic baroreceptors?
explanation: Stretching of aortic baroreceptors occurs due to increased blood pressure, causing a reflexive inhibition of vasoconstrictor centers in the medulla and vagal parasympathetic stimulation. This results in decreased vasoconstriction and decreased heart rate. Several mechanisms exist for regulating circulation peripherally via receptors and reflexes. The main receptor targets for regulation are the autonomic nervous system, which includes the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems. Sympathetic nerve fibers innervate both blood vessels and the heart with the overall function of increasing resistance via vasoconstriction and increasing cardiac activity, although sympathetic nervous system activation does have some vasodilatory function. Vasoconstriction is accomplished by activating alpha-1 receptors, while increased cardiac activity takes place by activating beta-1 receptors. Vasoconstriction takes place in both arteries and veins in order to increase peripheral resistance and transfer of blood from peripheral venous pools to heart. The parasympathetic system impacts circulation primarily via innervation to the heart, with activation of parasympathetic muscarinic receptors causing decreased heart rate and slightly decreased contractility. Reflexes within the circulatory system primarily utilize negative feedback mechanisms. The major circulatory reflexes are the baroreceptor reflexes. Baroreceptor reflexes utilize stretch receptors in large systemic arteries that are activated with increased arterial blood pressure, sending signals to the central nervous system which then provides feedback via the autonomic system to reduce blood pressure. The main baroreceptors are located in the aortic arch wall, as well as the carotid sinuses which are above the carotid bifurcation in the bilateral internal carotids. The aortic baroreceptors transmit efferent information via the vagus nerve to the tractus solitarius in the medulla, while the carotid sinus baroreceptors transmit information first via small Hering’s nerves and then the glossopharyngeal nerve to the tractus solitarius in the medulla. After arriving in the tractus solitarius, signals inhibit the vasoconstriction center in the medulla and stimulate the vagal parasympathetic center resulting in decreased peripheral resistance and decreased cardiac output, respectively. Normal reflex pathway function is a primary mechanism for maintaining stability in blood pressure during postural changes. For example, when transitioning from supine to standing there is a temporary decrease in perfusion to the carotid sinus baroreceptors, eliciting a rapid, reflexive compensation via sympathetic stimulation and parasympathetic inhibition that minimizes this decreased blood pressure to the carotids and brain. Animal models have demonstrated significant lability in blood pressure with routine daily activities in animals without baroreceptor function relative to those with preserved function. By nature, the baroreceptor reflex causes an oscillatory blood pressure cycle with high pressure causing reflexive decreases, and the reflexive decrease triggering a reflexive increase, and so on and so forth. The following are additional circulatory receptors and reflexes throughout the body. Abdominal compression reflex: Activation of baroreceptors causes increased sympathetic output, constricting abdominal muscle vascular pools, and increasing venous return to the heart. Atrial and pulmonary artery low-pressure receptors: Receptors that regulate reflexive blood pressure changes in response to blood volume changes. Atrial volume reflex: Increased atrial stretch causes dilation of afferent arterioles to the kidney, reduces antidiuretic hormone secretion from the hypothalamus, and releases an atrial natriuretic hormone, resulting in greater loss of fluid via the kidneys. Bainbridge reflex (atrial heart control reflex): Atrial stretch causes increased heart rate and contractility via sympathetic nervous system stimulation. Bezold-Jarisch reflex: Stimulation of chemoreceptors and mechanoreceptors in the left ventricle causes a parasympathetic response resulting in hypotension, bradycardia, and coronary artery dilation. Chemoreceptor reflex: Low blood pressure and other factors cause decreased partial oxygen pressure, increased hydrogen ion concentration, and increased carbon dioxide stimulating the carotid body and aortic body receptors. These receptors transmit signals to vasomotor centers via the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves, which increase respiratory drive, increase parasympathetic activity, and increase sympathetic activity if hypoxia is prolonged. Central nervous system (CNS) ischemic response: Thought to be due to brain ischemia manifesting as increased carbon dioxide levels, which increases sympathetic output resulting in increased vasoconstrictor and cardiac accelerator function. Ischemia may occur secondary to increased intracranial pressure, with the subsequent sympathetic ischemic response activating arterial baroreceptors and causing a reflexive decrease in heart rate. This increased blood pressure with decreased heart rate in the setting of increased intracranial pressure is commonly referred to as Cushing's reflex. Oculocardiac reflex: Stretch receptors activated by ocular pressure or stretch to surround structures send afferent signals via the ciliary nerve, ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, and then trigeminal nerve to the trigeminal ganglion. Increased parasympathetic tone results with efferent signals sent via the vagus nerve causing decreased heart rate.
rationales:
Decreased vasoconstriction and increased heart rate do not occur following baroreceptor stretch.
Answer C: Increased vasoconstriction and decreased heart rate can occur due to increased intracranial pressure, a response known as the Cushing reflex.
Answer D: Increased vasoconstriction and increased heart rate occur reflexively as a CNS ischemic response. This also may occur following low blood pressure that decreases baroreceptor firing.
bottomLine: Increased blood pressure causes stretching of baroreceptors primarily located in the aortic arch and carotid sinus. This leads to reflexive inhibition of vasoconstrictor centers in the medulla and vagal parasympathetic stimulation, resulting in decreased sympathetic vasoconstriction and decreased heart rate, respectively.
references: ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. “Circulation Regulation: Peripheral” Guyton and Hall. Textbook of Medical Physiology, 12th edition. Pages 204-211. Miller. Anesthesia, 8th edition. Pages 489-490.

Bezold-Jarisch reflex: Stimulation of chemoreceptors and mechanoreceptors in the left ventricle causes a parasympathetic response resulting in hypotension, bradycardia, and coronary artery dilation.

Chemoreceptor reflex: Low blood pressure and other factors cause decreased partial oxygen pressure, increased hydrogen ion concentration, and increased carbon dioxide stimulating the carotid body and aortic body receptors.

These receptors transmit signals to vasomotor centers via the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves, which increase respiratory drive, increase parasympathetic activity, and increase sympathetic activity if hypoxia is prolonged.

Central nervous system (CNS) ischemic response: Thought to be due to brain ischemia manifesting as increased carbon dioxide levels, which increases sympathetic output resulting in increased vasoconstrictor and cardiac accelerator function.

Ischemia may occur secondary to increased intracranial pressure, with the subsequent sympathetic ischemic response activating arterial baroreceptors and causing a reflexive decrease in heart rate.

This increased blood pressure with decreased heart rate in the setting of increased intracranial pressure is commonly referred to as Cushing's reflex.

Oculocardiac reflex: Stretch receptors activated by ocular pressure or stretch to surround structures send afferent signals via the ciliary nerve, ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, and then trigeminal nerve to the trigeminal ganglion.

Increased parasympathetic tone results with efferent signals sent via the vagus nerve causing decreased heart rate.
rationalesHtml:
• Answer B: Decreased vasoconstriction and increased heart rate do not occur following baroreceptor stretch.
  • Answer C: Increased vasoconstriction and decreased heart rate can occur due to increased intracranial pressure, a response known as the Cushing reflex.
  • Answer D: Increased vasoconstriction and increased heart rate occur reflexively as a CNS ischemic response. This also may occur following low blood pressure that decreases baroreceptor firing.
bottomLineHtml: Increased blood pressure causes stretching of baroreceptors primarily located in the aortic arch and carotid sinus. This leads to reflexive inhibition of vasoconstrictor centers in the medulla and vagal parasympathetic stimulation, resulting in decreased sympathetic vasoconstriction and decreased heart rate, respectively.

stem: Which of the following would MOST likely be found in a patient with cyanide toxicity?
explanation: The most common and reliable sign of cyanide toxicity is an anion gap metabolic acidosis. Cyanide primarily causes toxicity by impairing cellular aerobic respiration. The cyanide ion (CN-) binds to the ferric ion (Fe3+) in mitochondrial cytochrome-c oxidase, inhibiting the final stage of the electron transport chain. Depletion of cellular ATP and the lactic acid produced by anaerobic metabolism can lead to profound acidosis. Symptoms of cyanide toxicity include altered mental status, weakness, headaches, loss of consciousness, seizures, respiratory failure, and cardiac arrest. Blood cyanide levels will be elevated, although therapy should not be delayed for the laboratory result. The patients blood sample may appear "cherry red" due to normal circulating levels of oxygen with impaired utilization.
rationales:
Circulating oxygen is not impaired and cyanosis is a late finding.
Answer B: Oxygen is present, but it is unable to be utilized. Therefore, PaO2 will increase.
Answer C: Oxygen is present, but it is unable to be utilized. SvO2 will be increased.
bottomLine: The most common and reliable sign of cyanide toxicity is an anion gap metabolic acidosis.
trueLearnInsight: Anion gap is calculated by subtracting serum chloride and bicarbonate (anions) from serum sodium and potassium (cations). Anion gap = ([Na+] +[K+]) – ([Cl−] + [HCO3−]). In clinical practice, potassium is usually excluded.
references: Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 910, 1077. Miller Anesthesia, 8th edition, p. 2501. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Cyanide Toxicity: Dx"

stem: Patients with myotonic dystrophy have an increased risk of aspiration due to several mechanisms. Which of the following is NOT one of those mechanisms?
explanation: Myotonic dystrophy is characterized by gastric atony, not spasticity. Clinical manifestations of myotonic dystrophy are a result of delayed skeletal muscle relaxation after voluntary contraction. Two subtypes exist. Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is more common and can be congenital, child-onset, or most typically, autosomal dominant with adult-onset. Type 2 is rarer than type 1 and is typically associated with milder symptoms. Symptoms and associated findings of myotonic dystrophy include: - Muscle degeneration - Cataracts - Premature balding - Diabetes mellitus - Thyroid dysfunction - Adrenal insufficiency - Gonadal atrophy - Cardiac abnormalities (e.g., conduction dysfunction, cardiomyopathy, and mitral valve prolapse). Answers A & B & C: Respiratory muscle weakness can lead to a restrictive respiratory pattern and cause mild arterial hypoxemia, reduced ventilatory response to hypoxemia and hypercapnia, and an ineffective cough mechanism. Gastrointestinal muscle weakness can lead to gastric atony and delayed emptying, intestinal hypomotility (C), and pharyngeal muscle weakness. Each of these can contribute to an increased risk of pulmonary aspiration.
bottomLine: Patients with myotonic dystrophy have an increased risk of pulmonary aspiration due to gastric atony and delayed emptying, intestinal hypomotility, and pharyngeal muscle weakness.
references: Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 624. Miller, Miller’s Anesthesia, 7th edition, pp. 1605-1606.

stem: You are called to assess a 75-year-old woman in the preoperative area for light-headedness and low heart rate who already has an IV in place. When you arrive, she vomits and complains of severe dizziness with chest pain. Vital signs are obtained and reveal a blood pressure of 80/40 mmHg and a heart rate of 45 bpm. After ordering a stat ECG, what is the NEXT step in the management of this patient?
explanation: Timely identification and treatment of symptomatic bradycardia can truly be life-saving. This patient is experiencing bradycardia with resultant systemic hypotension, altered mental status, and angina. According to the American Heart Association advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) guidelines, the first-line treatment for symptomatic bradyarrhythmia is atropine, 1 mg IV, repeated every 3-5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg. If atropine is ineffective, the next step is to attempt transcutaneous pacing or administer dopamine or epinephrine by infusion. Illustration © TrueLearn, LLC
rationales:
Epinephrine is a second-line choice for bradycardia in adults. It is the first-line choice for children, however.
Answer C: Phenylephrine does not appear in the ACLS algorithms. If administered in this situation, it may result in reflex bradycardia, potentially further worsening perfusion.
Answer D: Transcutaneous pacing, while potentially helpful, is not the first-line treatment for bradycardia. It should be attempted only after failure of atropine to correct the bradyarrhythmia.
bottomLine: Symptomatic bradyarrhythmias are life-threatening and require immediate treatment. The first-line therapy for symptomatic bradycardia is atropine.
trueLearnInsight: Atropine is indicated for symptomatic bradycardia regardless of the conduction cause. However, it may be ineffective for second-degree Type II and third-degree blocks.

Ch. 86: Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation and Advanced Cardiac Life Support. American Heart Association. Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support Algorithms. Accesses 26 Jan 2022.

stem: Which of the following phases contributes the LARGEST volume of blood to the left ventricle during diastole?
explanation: Early rapid filling contributes the largest volume of blood during diastole. Diastole is the period of cardiac cycle between the aortic valve and mitral valve closure. During this time, the left ventricle is filling with blood from the left atrium. At the end of diastole, the volume in the left ventricle is referred to as the end-diastolic volume (or preload). There are four phases during diastole: isovolumetric relaxation, early rapid filling, diastasis (slow filling), and late rapid filling (atrial contraction). Isovolumetric relaxation: this phase begins with the closure of the aortic valve and continues till the opening of the mitral valve. During this time, the left ventricle is relaxing, however there is no change in the ventricular volume (isovolumetric). Early rapid filling: this phase begins with the opening of the mitral valve. The left ventricle begins to fill with blood from the left atrium. The flow of blood is driven by the transmitral pressure gradient. This phase contributes the largest volume of blood to the left ventricle during diastole. Diastasis (slow filling): as the left ventricle fills, the pressure difference between the left ventricle and atrium decrease. This slows down the filling considerably, and contributes approximately 5% of the preload. This phase occurs mid-diastole. Late rapid filling (atrial contraction): the left atrium contracts, ejecting additional blood into the left ventricle. This phase can contribute 15-20% of the preload. Atrial contraction is the last phase of diastole. The mitral valve closes after the atrial contraction.
rationales:
Late rapid filling (atrial contraction) contributes about 15% of the end-diastolic volume. Early rapid filling is the largest contributor of preload.
Answer C: Left ventricular relaxation is a period during diastole where there is no change in the left ventricular volume (isovolumetric).
Answer D: Slow filling (diastasis) occurs as the left ventricle fills and the pressures between atrium and ventricle become equal. This contributes about 5% of the preload.
bottomLine: Early rapid filling contributes the largest volume of blood during diastole. The phases of diastole are: isovolumetric relaxation, early rapid filling, diastasis, and atrial contraction.
trueLearnInsight: Atrial contraction normally contributes approximately 15% of the preload. In patients with poor left ventricular filling, as in diastolic dysfunction, the atrial contraction becomes very important.

stem: During exercise, oxygen diffusion in the lung is increased by which of the following mechanisms?

options.text: Increased capillary transit time in the lung
options.html: Increased capillary transit time in the lung

explanation: Oxygen diffusion is increased during exercise because of the recruitment of non-perfused capillary beds. Diffusion of a gas is a process by which the gas molecules move from an area of high partial pressure to an area of lower partial pressure. The movement of oxygen from the alveoli to the pulmonary capillary blood (and from the blood to the tissues) is passive. As oxygen moves from alveoli to the hemoglobin molecule, it must pass through: 1) the alveolar membrane (containing surfactant), 2) the capillary endothelium, 3) the plasma, 4) the red blood cell (RBC) membrane, and 5) the RBC intracellular fluid. Diffusion capacity of oxygen can be affected by changes to any of the factors mentioned above. The thickness of the alveolarcapillary membrane may affect the ability of oxygen to diffuse properly. During exercise, the total lung volume is increased, resulting in thinner, more distended alveoli. This increases the surface area of the lung allowing for greater oxygen diffusion. The tidal volume increases (up to 60%) with activity by encroaching into the inspiratory reserve volume. Therefore, during exercise, the inspiratory reserve is decreased. During exercise, increased pulmonary blood flow increases oxygen diffusion. The recruitment of capillary beds that were nonperfused at rest increases not only blood flow, but also the capillary cross-sectional area. Capillaries are recruited as groups, not individually. Areas with low capillary density are recruited first. This also improves the ventilation/perfusion ratio. RBC capillary transit time is the amount of time a single red blood cell spends in the capillary, where it is exposed to the alveolar gases. In other words, it is the amount of time a RBC has to pick up oxygen. At rest, the capillary transit time is approximately 0.8 seconds. Cardiac output is one of the factors that can change the capillary transit time. During exercise, the cardiac output increases causing a decrease in capillary transit time. There is no consensus on the impact of decreased transit time on oxygen diffusion during exercise. However, the minimum needed time for oxygen to diffuse into a RBC is 0.25 seconds.
rationales:
Capillary transit time decreases due to an increased cardiac output during exercise.
Answer B: Inspiratory reserve is decreased during exercise.
bottomLine: Exercise increases oxygen diffusion by increasing lung surface area (thinner, more distended alveoli) and by increasing blood flow (capillary recruitment).

stem: What is the basic type of cellular connection that allows for the fast propagation of an electrical signal in the cardiac myocyte?
explanation: Gap junctions allow for quick propagation of the electrical signal in the cardiac myocyte. Underlying a functional and efficient cardiac cycle is the concept of impulse propagation. Impulse propagation describes the flow of the electrical current generated by shifting ion concentrations leading to coordinated depolarization and repolarization of the cardiac myocyte. Dysfunction within the system can lead to a myriad of arrhythmias from benign to fatal. Basic propagation of the initial depolarization begins from the sinoatrial (SA) SA node, travels to the right atrium via the Bachmann bundle to excite the left atrium. The impulse travels through pathways to the atrioventricular (AV) node, down the bundle of His, and finally terminates in the Purkinje fibers. The ion channel has two main properties, chemical and electrical, driving the various gradients to propagate the signal. In addition, the channels are selective for a single type of ion, are voltagegated, and are time-dependent. At the cellular level, the majority of propagation of the initial signal occurs from cell-to-cell interaction via gap junctions. The gap junction allows for quick depolarization of the next cell in an organized fashion without delay seen in other types of cells within the body. The rest of the propagation occurs through the aforementioned specialized conduction fibers (e.g., bundle of His, Purkinje fibers). Damage to the myocardium can damage these communication pathways, thus disrupting the propagation of a normal signal leading to potential risks of arrhythmias.
rationales:
Anchoring junctions function in the adhesion to each other as well as other components of the extracellular matrix. This provides tissues with structural cohesion. Examples of these junctions include desmosomes, hemidesmosomes, and adherens junctions.
Answer C: Tight junctions function in the formation of barriers that regulate the movement of water and solutes.
Answer D: Tricellular junctions (TCJ) seal epithelia at three corners of corresponding cells around it. They bond together cells in a lattice-like formation leading to increased structural stability.
bottomLine: Gap junctions allow for quick propagation of the electrical signal in the cardiac myocyte.
references: ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. “Cardiac Physiology: Impulse Propagation” Kaplan’s Cardiac Anesthesia. Basic Electrophysiologic Principles in 2nd Edition. Pages 100-105. Kléber, Am et al. Basic Mechanisms of Cardiac Impulse Propagation and Associated Arrhythmias. Physiol Rev. 2004 April; 84: 431–488.

stem: What is the most common cation and anion found in both the extracellular (ECF) and intracellular fluid (ICF) compartments?

options.text: ECF cation = K+; ECF anion = Cl- ; ICF cation = Na+; ICF anion = phosphate and organic ions
options.html: ECF cation = K+; ECF anion = Cl- ; ICF cation = Na+; ICF anion = phosphate and organic ions

options.html: ECF cation = Na+; ECF anion = phosphate and organic ions; ICF cation = K+; ICF anion = Cl-

explanation: The major cation found in the ECF is sodium and the major cation found in the ICF is K+. Cell membrane proteins maintain this gradient by active transport. Action potentials and other intracellular processes function in relation to how this gradient is maintained. Electroneutrality must be maintained thus in the ECF compartment chloride ions balance the robust sodium concentration, and phosphate in addition to other organic ions balance the potassium inside the cell. Adult requirements for both sodium and potassium on a daily basis are approximately 75 mEq/kg and 40 mEq/kg, respectively. Fluids that most closely resemble that of plasma (Lactated Ringer, Normosol, Plasma-Lyte) tend to be the recommended resuscitation fluids for maintenance of appropriate electrolyte balances. Answers A & B: The major ECF cation is Na+, not K+.
rationales: the major ECF anion is Cl-, not phosphate and organic ions.
bottomLine: Sodium is the major extracellular cation while potassium is the major intracellular cation.
trueLearnInsight: Recall osmolality = ([Na+] * 2) + (Glucose/18) + (BUN/2.3) thus changes in either of these variable can lead to cellular shifts of water. This becomes particularly important with large sodium shifts or hyperglycemic states that can precipitate medical emergencies, such as seizures.
references: ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Renal Physiology: Water and Electrolytes" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 7th edition. Page 336

stem: In a patient breathing FiO2 of 0.30, the oxygen content in pulmonary capillary blood (CcO2), oxygen content in arterial blood (CaO2), and oxygen content in mixed venous blood (CvO2) expressed in mL of O2 per 100 mL of blood is • CcO2 = 21 • CaO2 = 20 • CvO2 = 15 Which of the following is the shunt fraction (Qs/Qt) for this patient?
explanation: The shunt fraction (Qs/Qt) can be calculated by using the venous admixture equation Qs/Qt = (CcO2 − CaO2) / (CcO2 − CvO2), where CcO2 is the oxygen content in pulmonary capillary blood, CaO2 is the oxygen content in arterial blood, and CvO2 is the oxygen content in mixed venous blood. The shunt fraction is the percentage of total cardiac output (Qt) that bypasses oxygenation from the lungs due to a right-to-left shunt. Even healthy patients have some component of right-to-left shunt due to the bronchial and thebesian circulation and atelectasis (intrapulmonary shunting). A normal shunt fraction is 2% to 3% but can be increased up to 10% in a healthy adult undergoing anesthesia primarily due to increased atelectasis and changes in ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) ratios. The term in the numerator (CcO2 − CaO2) represents the gap in oxygen content between pulmonary capillary blood and arterial blood, while the term in the denominator (CcO2 − CvO2) represents the maximal gap that could potentially occur if all of the mixed venous blood was shunted. The equation assumes that only 2 sources of blood mix together to result in the observed arterial blood, 1 source being mixed venous blood that has not been oxygenated at all (pure shunt) and fully oxygenated blood from the lungs. In reality, most of the difference between pulmonary capillary oxygenation and arterial oxygenation often comes from another source, namely alveoli with a low V/Q ratio. For example, a venous admixture of 5% could be explained by 10% to 15% of cardiac output perfusing poorly ventilated regions of the lungs. Venous admixture due to low V/Q will reverse by supplemental oxygen, but venous admixture due to pure shunt will not reverse by supplemental oxygen. Therefore, venous admixture, calculated by the Qs/Qt equation, represents all of the pure shunt plus some contribution from low V/Q alveoli. When venous admixture is due to perfusion of low V/Q alveoli, it will improve with supplemental oxygen, which is why many patients require some amount of supplemental oxygen to maintain high SpO2 after extubation.
rationales:
(21-20) / (21-15) = 1/6 ≈ 17%, not 5%. Five percent could be erroneously derived as the correct answer for this question by calculating (CaO2 − CvO2).
Answer C: (21-20) / (21-15) = 1/6 ≈ 17%, not 25%. Twenty-five percent could be erroneously calculated by taking (CaO2 − CvO2) / CaO2.
Answer D: (21-20) / (21-15) = 1/6 ≈ 17%, not 29%.
bottomLine: The shunt fraction (Qs/Qt) can be calculated by using the venous admixture equation Qs/Qt = (CcO2 −CaO2) / (CcO2 −CvO2), where CcO2 is the oxygen content in pulmonary capillary blood, CaO2 is the oxygen content in arterial blood, and CvO2 is the oxygen content in mixed venous blood. The shunt fraction is the percentage of total cardiac output (Qt) that bypasses oxygenation from the lungs due to a right-to-left shunt.

stem: Which of the following MOST accurately describes the mechanism of hyperglycemia in response to surgical stress?
explanation: Surgical stress leads to the increased secretion of glucose from counter-regulatory hormones and peripheral tissue resistance to insulin, resulting in hyperglycemia. Surgical stress and accidental injury lead to the increased secretion of the counter-regulatory hormones, including cortisol, catecholamines, and glucagon, resulting in an increased glucose production due to hepatic gluconeogenesis. The increase in glucose production, in conjunction with peripheral tissue resistance to insulin, leads to reduced glucose use and, subsequently, hyperglycemia. Serum insulin concentrations are inadequate to prevent hyperglycemia but do prevent ketosis from occurring. Hyperglycemia due to surgical stress ensures an adequate supply of glucose to glucose-consuming cells, including wound inflammatory and immune cells. Insulin resistance can persist for up to three weeks after elective cholecystectomy and for up to three years after major burn injuries. For patients in the intensive care unit, the severity of insulin resistance is associated with illness severity, body mass index, and degree of hypermetabolism.
rationales:
There is an increased secretion of catecholamines in response to surgical stress.
Answer B: Increased beta-2 adrenergic (not beta-1) stimulation leads to the acceleration of lipolysis through increased cyclic adenosine monophosphate concentrations, which stimulate the activity of hormone-sensitive lipase through protein kinase A. This accelerated lipolysis increases the supply of circulating free fatty acids.
Answer C: The increased secretion of counter-regulatory hormones, including glucagon, results in increased glucose production secondary to hepatic gluconeogenesis, not glycogenesis.
bottomLine: Surgical stress leads to increased production of counter-regulatory hormones, including catecholamines, glucagon, and cortisol. This results in an increased production of glucose from hepatic gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword: "Stress and carbohydrate metabolism" Gropper MA, et al. Miller’s Anesthesia. Ch. 106: Nutrition and Metabolomics. Section: Carbohydrate Metabolism. 9th edition.

stem: In a patient with a left-dominant coronary circulation, the following flow pattern in the right coronary artery would most likely correspond to which of the following?
explanation: A diastolic preponderance of coronary blood flow is normal in the left ventricle, not the right ventricle. This pattern suggests chronic pulmonary hypertension. Because of the different intraventricular pressures developing during systole, perfusion of the left ventricle - particularly the left ventricular subendocardium, takes place almost entirely during diastole. Whereas the right ventricle is perfused throughout the cardiac cycle. However, in cases of chronic pulmonary hypertension a "left ventricularization" of the right ventricle occurs, such that the right ventricle becomes hypertrophied, suffers a decrease in blood flow and blood flow reserve, and its perfusion becomes predominantly diastolic (which also means it will depend on aortic diastolic pressure to maintain coronary blood flow). Also similarly to the left ventricle, when the right ventricle becomes dilated oxygen demand increases. Recall that wall tension, one of the main determinants of oxygen demand, is proportional to the radius by the law of Laplace. The figure here shows a diagrammatic representation of normal blood flow in the left and right coronary arteries. For the purpose of simplicity, it is assumed that the patient has a left dominance, so that the right coronary artery represents purely right ventricular coronary blood flow pattern. Answers B & C & D: Under these conditions, the right ventricle is perfused throughout the cardiac cycle.
bottomLine: The normal right ventricle is perfused throughout the cardiac cycle. Flow to the left ventricle (and the right ventricle in cases of chronic pulmonary hypertension) is largely confined to diastole.
