stem: Which of the following combination of rhythm, defibrillator type, and energy level is CORRECT?

options.text: Atrial fibrillation, 360 Joules with biphasic waveform
options.html: Atrial fibrillation, 360 Joules with biphasic waveform

options.text: Atrial flutter, 100 Joules with monophasic waveform
options.html: Atrial flutter, 100 Joules with monophasic waveform

options.text: Ventricular fibrillation, 200 Joules with monophasic waveform
options.html: Ventricular fibrillation, 200 Joules with monophasic waveform

options.text: Ventricular tachycardia, 360 Joules with biphasic waveform
options.html: Ventricular tachycardia, 360 Joules with biphasic waveform

explanation: For atrial flutter, 100 Joules of monophasic shock should be delivered. Time from cardiac arrest until the first shock administration affects survival significantly and defibrillation or cardioversion has an integral role in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). For ventricular fibrillation (VF) and ventricular tachycardia (VT), directcurrent (DC) cardioversion is the therapy of choice. Most modern defibrillators are biphasic, with older models being monophasic and requiring a larger energy level. The energy level for defibrillation in adults is 200 Joules for biphasic shocks or 360 joules for monophasic shocks. After the first shock, if VF or VT does not terminate, the subsequent energy level should be kept the same or may be increased. Each shock should be inter-spaced with CPR for at least 2 minutes and successive shocks without CPR have not been shown to improve survival. In cases of atrial fibrillation, 100 to 200 Joules with monophasic shocks or 100 to 120 Joules of biphasic shocks should be administered for cardioversion. In cases of atrial flutter, 50 to 100 Joules of monophasic shocks should be administered. When possible, biphasic defibrillators should be used over monophasic defibrillators due to their better success rates at arrhythmia termination. Compared to manual defibrillators, automated external defibrillators analyze the rhythm transmitted by the pads placed on the chest and determine if defibrillation is indicated. Per the 2015 ACLS guidelines, it is acceptable to use the manufacturer's recommended dose for the first shock for ventricular fibrillation with a biphasic defibrillator. Note that for unwitnessed cardiac arrests, for arrests outside of the hospital or greater than 5 minutes since arrest, CPR should be initiated for up to 3 minutes prior to the first shock. Lastly, note that pulseless electrical activity (PEA) and asystole are nonshockable rhythms. Instead, epinephrine and uninterrupted CPR should be continued.
rationales: For atrial fibrillation, 100 to 200 Joules with a monophasic waveform or 100 to 120 Joules with a biphasic waveform should be used. Answers C & D: Ventricular fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia should be treated with 200 Joules of biphasic waveform or 360 Joules of monophasic waveform.
bottomLine: Monophasic defibrillators require more energy level than biphasic defibrillators. For biphasic shocks: • VF/VT: 200 J • Atrial fibrillation: 120 J For monophasic shocks: • VF/VT: 360 J • Atrial fibrillation: 200 J

stem: Which of the following does NOT have an effect on left ventricular myocardial oxygen supply?
explanation: Myocardial oxygen supply has several determinants. It is associated with oxygen content and blood flow. It is unaffected by left ventricular systolic pressure. First, the oxygen content is determined to evaluate oxygen availability or supply: CaO2 = (Hgb * 1.34 * SaO2) + (0.003 * PaO2) Where: CaO2 = arterial oxygen content (mL/dL), Hgb = hemoglobin (g/dL), SaO2 = oxygen saturation, PaO2 = arterial partial pressure of oxygen (mm Hg). Oxygen dissolved in arterial blood (0.003 x PaO2) raises the total value by only a small amount. If PaO2 is increased, there is little change in CaO2 and it is therefore considered of little significance by most when determining oxygen content. Optimizing Hgb amount is one way to ensure maximal oxygen content. Secondly, myocardial blood supply is determined by coronary blood flow (CBF), which has its own set of modifying components: 1) Heart rate: Left ventricular blood supply from the coronary arteries occurs primarily during diastole. A slower heart rate means more time is spent in diastole which allows more time for CBF to the left ventricle. 2) Coronary perfusion pressure: Coronary perfusion pressure (CPP) is represented as the difference between the aortic diastolic pressure (AoDP) and the left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP). CPP = AoDP - LVEDP 3) Coronary vascular resistance (CVR): Increased CVR such as from vasospasm or atherosclerosis worsens myocardial oxygen supply. Providing vasodilation with medications such as nitroglycerin improves CBF. Coronary blood flow is therefore represented by the following equation: CBF = CPP / CVR, or, CBF = (AoDP – LVEDP) / CVR. Myocardial oxygen extraction also plays a role in supply, but this value is usually at its maximum value and changes very little under times of stress. Left ventricular systolic pressure (LVSP) is more often associated with changing the myocardial oxygen demand (not supply) by changing afterload. An elevated LVSP will increase wall stress and require more myocardial oxygen.
rationales:
Coronary perfusion pressure (CPP) is represented as the difference between the aortic diastolic pressure (AoDP) and the left ventricular end diastolic pressure (LVEDP).
Answer B: Increased coronary vascular resistance such as from vasospasm or atherosclerosis worsens myocardial oxygen supply. Providing vasodilation with medications such as nitroglycerin improves CBF.
Answer C: Left ventricular blood supply from the coronary arteries occurs primarily during diastole. A slower heart rate means more time is spent in diastole which allows more time for CBF to the left ventricle.
Answer D: Optimizing Hgb amount is one way to ensure maximal oxygen content.
bottomLine: Myocardial oxygen supply is affected by AoDP, LVEDP, heart rate, Hgb, and CVR. Left ventricular systolic pressure affects myocardial oxygen demand.

stem: A 35-year-old man with acromegaly presents for transsphenoidal endoscopic resection of a pituitary adenoma. Which of the following is MOST LIKELY present on preoperative evaluation?
explanation: Patients with acromegaly may present with peripheral neuropathy. The anterior pituitary is responsible for the production and release of six hormones, including growth hormone, thryoid stimulating hormone, adrenocorticotropic hormone, prolactin, and gonadotropins (follicle-stimulating and luteinizing hormones). Overactivity of each of these hormones can cause systemic changes. Growth hormone is a peptide trophic hormone that promotes cellular hypertrophy, proliferation, and regeneration. Its excess causes acromegaly, which causes connective tissue, bone, and internal organ enlargement. Acromegaly results in enlargement of connective tissue, bone, and visceral organs. This can result in an increased risk of central or obstructive sleep apnea, difficult airways due to macroglossia and swollen epiglottides, hyperglycemia, hypertension, congestive heart failure, valvular disease, coronary artery disease, diabetes, hypothyroidism, and peripheral neuropathy.
rationales:
Hypertension is a more likely presentation due to extrinsic compression of vasculature from cellular hypertrophy.
Answer B: Skeletal, soft tissue, and connective tissue overgrowth results in macroglossia, prognathism, enlarged epiglottis, swollen vocal cords, and recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis.
Answer C: Hyperglycemia is a more likely presentation due to reduced hepatic uptake of glucose from excess growth hormone.
bottomLine: Growth hormone is a peptide hormone made in the anterior pituitary that promotes anabolic functions for musculoskeletal and visceral organ development. Growth hormone excess results in acromegaly, which can cause significant airway and cardiovascular changes.
references: ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. “Endocrine Physiology: Pituitary” Miller Anesthesia, 8th edition. Pg 1130-1131.

options.html: A reduction of blood flow in the hepatic artery

options.text: An increase in adenosine concentration in the liver
options.html: An increase in adenosine concentration in the liver

explanation: The liver is one of the few organs in the body that receives a dual blood supply. It is supplied by both the hepatic artery and the portal vein. Typically, the hepatic artery supplies 25% of the hepatic blood flow while the portal vein supplies 75%. Blood flow in the liver is autonomically regulated and based on pre-portal organ venous return. This system is termed the hepatic arterial buffer response (HABR) which is responsible for maintaining constant hepatic blood flow. The system functions in a manner such that when portal venous blood flow decreases, the hepatic artery vasodilates to maintain perfusion. The main determinant controlling this hepatic blood flow is adenosine. It is produced in the space of Mall which surrounds the hepatic vasculature and diffuses into the portal vein. When the portal venous blood flow decreases, the adenosine accumulates resulting in vasodilation of the hepatic artery increasing blood flow to the liver by the hepatic artery.
rationales:
A reduction in blood flow in the portal vein will lead to an increase in liver adenosine.
Answer B: A reduction of blood flow in the portal vein will lead to an increase in blood flow in the hepatic artery.
Answer D: A reduction of blood flow in the portal vein will lead to local liver arteriole dilation.
bottomLine: Decreased blood flow through the portal vein results in an increase of liver adenosine, local arteriole dilation, and increased hepatic artery blood flow.
references: ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. “Blood Flow: Splanchnic And Hepatic” Stoelting's anesthesia and co-existing disease. Diseases of the liver and biliary tract in 7th ed. E-book. Pages 345-358.

stem: Respiratory changes found in the obstetric patient include which of the following?

options.text: A decrease in inspiratory reserve volume
options.html: A decrease in inspiratory reserve volume

options.text: A decrease in the anteroposterior and transverse diameter of the thoracic cage
options.html: A decrease in the anteroposterior and transverse diameter of the thoracic cage

explanation: Many respiratory changes occur in the obstetric patient due to both anatomic and hormonal alterations. As the pregnancy progresses, the diaphragm moves more cephalad which causes a decrease in the functional residual capacity. In order to compensate for this change, the thoracic rib cage increases in anteroposterior and transverse diameter which aids to cause only a slight decrease in the total lung capacity overall. The functional residual capacity decreases by about 20-30% as does the expiratory reserve volume and residual volume. In addition, there is an increase in the inspiratory reserve volume. Airway resistance remains unchanged as progesterone relaxes the bronchiolar smooth muscle which combats the increased airway resistance due to upper airway edema. These changes contribute to a rapid desaturation during apnea and necessitate prompt airway intervention to avoid complications.
rationales:
An increased inspiratory reserve volume is usually seen in the obstetric patient.
Answer B: Obstetric patients have an increased anteroposterior and transverse diameter of the thoracic rib cage to offset the decrease in the functional residual capacity seen from the cephalad movement of the diaphragm.
Answer C: Progesterone causes relaxation of the bronchiolar smooth muscle and mitigates the increase in airway resistance from upper airway edema.
bottomLine: Respiratory changes in the parturient include a cephalad movement of the diaphragm with a concomitant increase in the anteroposterior and transverse diameter of the thoracic rib cage. There is a decrease in the functional residual capacity and its components as well as an increase in the inspiratory reserve volume. Airway resistance remains relatively unchanged.
references: Barash Anesthesia. Obstetrical Anesthesia in Seventh Edition. Page1146. ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Maternal Physiology: Respiratory Anatomy"

stem: A 50-year-old man weighing 70 kg is in the critical care unit after a motor vehicle accident in which he experienced multiple rib fractures, thoracic spine fractures, and pulmonary contusion bilaterally. He is currently intubated and mechanically ventilated. Which of the following is MOST true regarding the renal effects of positive pressure ventilation?

options.text: Positive pressure ventilation increases sympathetic output, which will increase urine output
options.html: Positive pressure ventilation increases sympathetic output, which will increase urine output

options.text: Secretion of antidiuretic hormone would be greater if the patient did not require positive pressure ventilation
options.html: Secretion of antidiuretic hormone would be greater if the patient did not require positive pressure ventilation

options.text: Tidal volume of 6 mL/kg could decrease renal injury by decreasing cytokine release
options.html: Tidal volume of 6 mL/kg could decrease renal injury by decreasing cytokine release

explanation: Decreasing the tidal volume to 6 mL/kg (lung-protective strategy) could decrease the risk of renal injury related to positive pressure in the patient in this question by decreasing cytokine release. Multiple reports of studies have linked renal and lung injury together through multiple mechanisms. The ARDSnet trial provided evidence that lung-protective ventilation decreases the incidence of hemodynamic, coagulopathic, and renal complications with a lung-protective strategy. Unfortunately, renal effects secondary to mechanical ventilation are not as simplistic as alterations in cytokine release. Strategies employed to target specific renal consequences from positive pressure ventilation have not been proven effective. Renal effects from mechanical ventilation involve 3 broad categories: hemodynamic, neurohormonal, and biochemical. Induction of positive pressure ventilation affects hemodynamics by decreasing preload and increasing right ventricular afterload (both of which decrease cardiac output and renal blood flow) while promoting increased venous pressure, all of which have deleterious effects on the kidneys. Positive pressure ventilation also results in an increase in sympathetic nervous system output, which secondarily results in an increase in renin release through beta-1 receptor stimulation with resultant release of angiotensin-2 and aldosterone. This results in vasoconstriction with salt and water retention, which can decrease urine output. There is also an increase in the release of antidiuretic hormone (also seen with surgical stress), which increases free water reabsorption and decreases urine output; however, this is a minor component. Finally, there is a decrease in atrial natriuretic peptide, which decreases natriuresis and vasodilation. Biochemically, positive pressure ventilation induces cytokine release, which can cause endothelial activation, increase vascular permeability, and result in apoptosis of renal epithelial cells. The pattern of ventilation can have alterations in the amount of cytokine release and resultant renal injury as previously discussed regarding the ARDSnet trial. There is also evidence that positive pressure ventilation increases the release of nitric oxide and enhances nitric oxide synthase activity. The breakdown products of nitric oxide cause oxidative damage and increased vascular permeability and can result in cellular apoptosis.
rationales:
Sympathetic output is increased with positive pressure ventilation; however, this leads to decreased urine output.
Answer B: Antidiuretic hormone secretion would be decreased compared to a patient on positive pressure ventilation.
bottomLine: Positive pressure ventilation exerts deleterious effects on renal function via alterations in hemodynamics, neurohormonal secretion, and biochemical mediator release.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Mechanical Ventilation: Renal Effects" Koyner JL, et al. Mechanical Ventilation and Lung-Kidney Interaction. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2008 Mar;3(2):562-570.

stem: A pregnant 25-year-old woman with a history of chronic seizure disorder at 35 weeks gestational age is currently being managed on phenytoin. Which of the following is MOST TRUE regarding the pharmacokinetics of phenytoin in this patient compared to a non-pregnant patient?

options.text: The concentration of phenytoin bound to serum proteins will increase
options.html: The concentration of phenytoin bound to serum proteins will increase

options.text: The clearance of phenytoin will decrease
options.html: The clearance of phenytoin will decrease

options.text: The free concentration of phenytoin will increase
options.html: The free concentration of phenytoin will increase

options.text: The total phenytoin needed to achieve a therapeutic target range will increase
options.html: The total phenytoin needed to achieve a therapeutic target range will increase

explanation: Changes in plasma protein binding during pregnancy will require the dosing of phenytoin and other highly protein-bound medications to be modified. Because plasma albumin concentrations can decrease to around 70% of normal, the free concentration of drug that is available to bind will increase, resulting in less drug overall needed to achieve a desired therapeutic goal. The distribution of medications during pregnancy will change due to a variety of factors, including an increased cardiac output, and increased total body water, and a decrease in plasma protein binding. The increased cardiac output will result in more rapid delivery of medications to the peripheral circulation. Thus medications such as neuromuscular blocking drugs, that have a peripheral site of action, may have a more rapid onset in a pregnant patient though this effect is of uncertain clinical significance. The expansion of total body water by around 8 liters over the course of pregnancy, corresponding to around a 40% increase in circulating plasma volume. This volume expansion will cause an increase in the volume of distribution of certain hydrophilic medications. The decrease in plasma protein binding will tend to have the greatest effect on the pharmacokinetics of a pregnant woman when compared to these other changes in medication distribution. As mentioned above, plasma albumin levels will tend to decrease to around 70% of normal levels. This is combined with the fact that pregnant women have an increased concentration of free fatty acids and other endogenous substances that will tend to compete with protein-bound medications in binding to albumin, further decreasing their effective volume of distribution. The net effect of this is to lead to an increased concentration of circulating free drug and a decreased concentration of drug bound to protein following an equivalent dose of a protein-bound medication in a pregnant woman when compared to a similar non-pregnant patient. Chronic administration of a drug will tend to be partially compensated by increased compensatory clearance mechanisms, though the total dose that is necessary to achieve a therapeutic serum level will tend to decrease. Of note, it is because of this effect that it is important to recognize what is actually being measured when monitoring serum concentrations of protein-bound medications in pregnancy. If the free drug concentration is being measured, dose titrations are relatively easy. If, however, the total serum concentration is being measured, the dose calculation becomes slightly more complex and will likely need to account for serum albumin levels as well.
rationales:
The concentration of phenytoin that is bound to serum proteins will tend to decrease in pregnancy.
Answer B: In chronically administered drugs that are highly protein-bound, there will be a modest increase in plasma clearance to compensate for the increased free drug concentrations.
Answer D: Given the decreased effective volume of distribution due to decreased plasma protein-binding, the total drug needed to achieve a clinical effect will decrease.
bottomLine: Plasma albumin concentrations will tend to decrease to around 70% of normal ranges during pregnancy. This will result in an increased concentration of free drug in the serum, as well as a decreased concentration of the drug that is bound to serum proteins. This results in less total drug that is needed to achieve a certain clinical effect.
references: ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Maternal Physiology: Protein Binding Of Drugs" Chestnut's Obstetric Anesthesia. Changes in Drug Disposition and Effect in 5th Edition. Pages 304 - 305.

stem: Which of the following BEST describes the mechanism of action of cytochrome p450?
explanation: Cytochrome p450 is a heme protein that utilizes molecular oxygen to oxidize organic compounds. Cytochrome p450 is not a single enzyme, but rather consists of a group of closely related proteins that are embedded in the endoplasmic reticulum. The structure of cytochrome p450 consists of iron (Fe), which serves as a binding site for oxygen molecules. Metabolism by cytochrome p450 has been extensively studied, and is involved in the oxidation of thousands of diverse drugs and chemicals. One atom of molecular oxygen is used to oxidize the drug, while the other atom is combined with hydrogen atoms from NADPH to form water. The liver is the principal site for drug metabolism. For many drugs, metabolism occurs in two phases. Phase I involves modifying the drug through oxidation, reduction, or hydrolysis. These reactions typically inactivate the drug. Phase II involves conjugation, where a molecule (glucuronic acid, sulfate) is added to the drug to make it more easily excreted from the kidneys and liver. Cytochrome p450 is the most important enzyme system in phase I and catalyzes the oxidation of many drugs.
rationales:
Conjugation is part of phase II metabolism, where molecules are added to the drug to make it more readily excreted. Cytochrome p450 is involved with phase I oxidation.
Answer B: Hydrolysis is part of phase I, but is not mediated by p450 group.
Answer D: Reduction is part of phase I metabolism. However, cytochrome p450 catalyzes oxidation in phase I.
bottomLine: Cytochrome p450 is involved in phase I metabolism by oxidizing many drugs.
trueLearnInsight: Chronic barbiturate use increases cytochrome p450 activity. As a result, the metabolism of drugs by p450 is increased (as seen with benzodiazepines).
references: Gibson G and Skett P. Introduction to Drug Metabolism. 3rd Edition. 2001. Pages 39-64. Groves JT and Han YZ. Cytochrome P450. 2nd Edition. 1995. Pages 3-48. Tashjian A, Armstrong E. Principles of Pharmacology: The Pathophysiologic Basis of Drug Therapy. 2011. 3rd Ed. Pages 173-175. Vaz A and Coon M. On the Mechanism of Action of Cytochrome P450: Evaluation of Hydrogen Abstraction in OxygenDependent Alcohol Oxidation. Biochemistry. 1994;33:6442-6449. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. stem: An infusion of cardioplegia is given via the anterograde cardioplegia line for coronary artery bypass surgery. A sample of blood is taken and the myocardial consumption is found to be 2 mL O2/minute per 100 g. In addition, the coronary blood flow (CBF) is 10 mL/min per 100 g according to the perfusionist. What is the gradient between arterial and venous oxygen content of coronary blood flow?
explanation: Myocardial oxygen consumption is determined by coronary blood flow and the difference between the arterial and venous concentrations of oxygen. Plainly stated, it is the flow of blood through the coronaries multiplied by the amount of oxygen extracted. Thus, to determine the myocardial oxygen consumption one needs to determine the CBF, arterial oxygen content, and venous oxygen content of coronary blood. The equation for determining myocardial oxygen consumption is as follows: MVO2 = CBF * (AO2 – VO2), where MVO2 equals myocardial oxygen consumption, CBF equals coronary blood flow, AO2 equals arterial oxygen contents and VO2 equals venous oxygen contents. In this question, the term (AO2 – VO2) is solved for, yielding a gradient of 0.2 mL O2/mL blood.
rationales: Using the equation for myocardial oxygen consumption, which is MVO2 = CBF * (AO2 – VO2), yields a gradient of 0.2 mL O2/mL of blood when MVO2 = 2 mL O2/minute per 100 g and CBF = 10 mL/min per 100 g. Answers B & C: Using the equation for myocardial oxygen consumption, which is MVO2 = CBF * (AO2 – VO2), yields a gradient of 0.2 mL O2/mL of blood when MVO2 = 2 mL O2/minute per 100 g and CBF = 10 mL/min per 100 g
bottomLine: The equation for determining myocardial oxygen consumption is MVO2 = CBF * (AO2 – VO2), where MVO2 equals myocardial oxygen consumption, CBF equals coronary blood flow, AO2 equals arterial oxygen content and VO2 equals venous oxygen content.
references: ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. “Cardiac Physiology: Fick Principle" Klabunde, R. Cardiovascular Physiology Concepts. Pages 85-87. Miller Anesthesia. Cardiac Physiology in 7th edition. Pages 478-479.

stem: Which of the following is TRUE regarding acetylcholine synthesis and release at the neuromuscular junction?

options.text: Acetylcholine is recycled back into the neuron via nicotinic acetylcholine receptor channels
options.html: Acetylcholine is recycled back into the neuron via nicotinic acetylcholine receptor channels

options.text: Acetylcholine synthesis is catalyzed by choline acetyltransferase in the presynaptic neuron
options.html: Acetylcholine synthesis is catalyzed by choline acetyltransferase in the presynaptic neuron

options.text: Butyrylcholinesterase rapidly metabolizes acetylcholine to choline and acetic acid within the neuromuscular junction
options.html: Butyrylcholinesterase rapidly metabolizes acetylcholine to choline and acetic acid within the neuromuscular junction

options.text: The influx of sodium leads to the release of acetylcholine from presynaptic vesicles
options.html: The influx of sodium leads to the release of acetylcholine from presynaptic vesicles

explanation: Acetylcholine (ACh) is synthesized in the presynaptic terminal by acetylation of choline with acetyl-CoA via choline acetyltransferase in the cytoplasm. Large amounts of ACh molecules are then stored together within vesicles near the cell membrane. After propagation of an action potential (via sodium channels), there is activation of voltage-gated calcium channels at the nerve terminal and calcium influx leading to "docking" of the ACh vesicles to SNARE proteins. The two fuse and ACh is released via exocytosis. A portion of the ACh molecules activate the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, although a large amount of ACh is rapidly metabolized by acetylcholinesterase to form acetate and choline. Choline is recycled back into the nerve terminal.
rationales:
Acetylcholine is rapidly broken down by acetylcholinesterase in the synapse into acetate and choline. Choline is recycled back into the presynaptic neuron. Unlike norepinephrine, there is no reuptake of acetylcholine and it must be synthesized constantly.
Answer C: Butyrylcholinesterase, also known as pseudocholinesterase or plasma cholinesterase, is not found significant amounts in neurons or in the neuromuscular junction. As the name implies, this enzyme is primarily found in the plasma. It is responsible for the metabolism of a variety of compounds, including succinylcholine, mivacurium, and ester local anesthetics.
Answer D: Calcium influx is required for acetylcholine release via SNARE protein-mediated exocytosis into the synaptic cleft.
bottomLine: Acetylcholine is synthesized in a variety of neuron terminals via choline acetyltransferase. The acetylcholine molecules are stored in vesicles which are released after propagation of an action potential leads to calcium influx. Specialized docking proteins (SNARE) are required for exocytosis.
references: ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Neuromuscular Physiology: Acetylcholine Synthesis and Release" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 7th edition, pp. 368-370, 526-527.

• Answer A: Acetylcholine is rapidly broken down by acetylcholinesterase in the synapse into acetate and choline. Choline is recycled back into the presynaptic neuron. Unlike norepinephrine, there is no reuptake of acetylcholine and it must be synthesized constantly.
  • Answer C: Butyrylcholinesterase, also known as pseudocholinesterase or plasma cholinesterase, is not found significant amounts in neurons or in the neuromuscular junction. As the name implies, this enzyme is primarily found in the plasma. It is responsible for the metabolism of a variety of compounds, including succinylcholine, mivacurium, and ester local anesthetics.
  • Answer D: Calcium influx is required for acetylcholine release via SNARE protein-mediated exocytosis into the synaptic cleft.
bottomLineHtml:
Acetylcholine is synthesized in a variety of neuron terminals via choline acetyltransferase. The acetylcholine molecules are stored in vesicles which are released after propagation of an action potential leads to calcium influx.

Specialized docking proteins (SNARE) are required for exocytosis.

stem: Which of the following is a TRUE statement regarding the pathophysiology and/or anesthetic management of a myasthenia gravis patient?

options.text: Presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels are affected
options.html: Presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels are affected

options.text: Rocuronium dosage will likely need to be increased
options.html: Rocuronium dosage will likely need to be increased

options.text: Succinylcholine dosage will likely need to be increased
options.html: Succinylcholine dosage will likely need to be increased

explanation: Succinylcholine dosage will likely need to be increased (1.5-2 mg/kg) for proper intubating conditions secondary to a decreased number of functional acetylcholine receptors. Myasthenia gravis patients have autoantibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and will likely require increased succinylcholine dosage for intubating conditions. Lambert-Eaton (myasthenic syndrome) patients have IgG antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels and typically require decreased succinylcholine dosage. Both patients would require decreased dosages of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers.
rationales:
This disease is not to be confused with Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, which is characterized by IgG antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels. In Lambert-Eaton syndrome, succinylcholine dosage would likely need to be decreased, as these patients are very sensitive to depolarizing and non-depolarizing muscle relaxants.
Answer B: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder in which autoantibodies exist against the alpha-subunit of the muscletype nicotinic postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors, that causes neuromuscular transmission failure with associated muscle weakness and fatigue.
Answer C: Non-depolarizing muscle relaxant doses should be decreased.
bottomLine: Succinylcholine dosage for intubation will likely need to be increased in myasthenia gravis patients.

stem: Which of the following statements about acute mountain sickness is INCORRECT?

options.text: A decrease in CSF bicarbonate offsets the decrease in PaCO2 from hyperventilation
options.html: A decrease in CSF bicarbonate offsets the decrease in PaCO2 from hyperventilation

options.text: Cerebral edema may occur due to hyperemia and hypoxia
options.html: Cerebral edema may occur due to hyperemia and hypoxia

options.text: Pulmonary edema is more likely in patients with preexisting pulmonary hypertension
options.html: Pulmonary edema is more likely in patients with preexisting pulmonary hypertension

options.text: Spironolactone is the preferred medication for prophylaxis
options.html: Spironolactone is the preferred medication for prophylaxis

explanation: Acetazolamide, not spironolactone, is effective for prophylaxis against symptoms of acute mountain sickness (AMS). Upon ascent to a high altitude, PaO2 and PaCO2 will significantly drop due to decreased atmospheric pressure and the resultant changes in respiratory drive. For example, at approximately 4500 meters, a PaO2 of 35-40 mm Hg and PaCO2 of 30-32 mm Hg could be expected. The initial hypoxia will trigger peripheral chemoreceptors to promote ventilation (and much more slowly, hematocrit will increase to improve oxygen delivery). However, this leads to a respiratory alkalosis due to increased minute ventilation. An adaptive mechanism to offset this alkalosis is the gradual reduction in plasma bicarbonate (primarily from increased secretion) which is preceded by a decrease in CSF bicarbonate. After 2-3 days of disequilibrium, the stimulation of peripheral chemoreceptors by hypoxia goes unopposed once enough bicarbonate ions have passed into the blood stream from CSF and the pH of the CSF is restored to sea level values. Acute mountain sickness or high altitude sickness is a result of continuous exposure to hypoxia. The most common symptoms include headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, ataxia, peripheral edema, and dyspnea. Prophylaxis is recommended prior to any ascent to greater than 3000 meters above sea level. Prophylaxis may include a “staged ascent” in which several days are spent at increasing heights until the goal is reached. Also, the avoidance of any respiratory depressants is recommended so hypoxic pulmonary drive is not blunted. Acetazolamide (a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) is a recommended pharmacologic AMS prophylactic measure as it augments the hypoxic ventilatory response promoting urinary bicarbonate loss. Treatment of AMS and its symptoms is primarily by altitude descent but can also include supplemental oxygen administration, dexamethasone administration (though symptoms often return once discontinued), and acetazolamide (especially for AMS-related insomnia).
rationales:
Decreased CSF bicarbonate is an adaptive mechanism that helps restore CSF pH to normal values in the setting of a respiratory alkalosis caused by high altitude.
Answer B: High altitude cerebral edema (HACE) may be caused by a significant increase in cerebral blood flow leading to hyperemia in the setting of hypoxia. It usually presents in the setting of preexisting AMS or HAPE and is usually recognized due to altered consciousness and/or ataxia. Treatment should be immediate descent and high FiO2. A hyperbaric bag can be placed around the entire body. This pressurized system increases barometric pressure and is useful in the treatment of all forms of AMS if descent is not immediately possible.
Answer C: High altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE) is thought to be caused by increased pressure in the pulmonary vasculature. The increased pulmonary capillary permeability in patients with preexisting pulmonary hypertension may worsen their predisposition to developing HAPE. This is due to the further increase in pulmonary vascular resistance from hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV). Nifedipine and inhaled β2-agonists are used as prophylaxis and treatment to reduce HPV (most vasodilators impair HPV). Treatment strategy includes supplemental oxygen with gradual descent to lower altitudes.
Answer D: Acetazolamide, not spironolactone, is the diuretic recommended for AMS prophylaxis.
bottomLine: Ascent to high altitudes leads to hypoxia and a resultant respiratory alkalosis. However, the body is able to acutely adapt over 2-3 days and reequilibrates PaO2, PaCO2, arterial pH, and CSF pH primarily by changes in ventilatory drive and increased bicarbonate excretion. However, a person may experience AMS, HAPE, and/or HACE prior to achieving an equilibrium driven by hypoxic ventilatory drive. AMS presents with non-specific symptoms including headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, and malaise. Prophylaxis can be accomplished with staged ascent and acetazolamide. Treatment includes descent, supplemental oxygen, and dexamethasone. More severe manifestations include HAPE and HACE, both of which should be treated with descent and supplemental oxygen.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "High Altitude Sickness" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 240-243. Miller, Miller's Anesthesia, 7th edition, pp. 2488-2490, 2502-2505. James M, White J. Anesthetic Considerations at Moderate Altitude. Anesthesia Analgesia (1984); 63: 1097-1105.

stem: A 42-year-old woman with status post ovarian mass resection is shivering in the postanesthesia care unit. She is noted to have a temperature of 33.6°C. What is the MOST effective intraoperative method to rewarm hypothermic patients?
explanation: Forced-air warming is the most effective method to reduce heat loss during anesthesia. Hypothermia increases the risk of postoperative infection, myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, bleeding, and poor wound healing. The duration of stay in the postanesthesia care unit (PACU) is increased on average by 40 to 90 minutes for hypothermic patients. Prevention of hypothermia is vital to minimize these risks. Identifying hypothermia is the first step to preventing and treating hypothermia. The American Society of Anesthesiologists guidelines require temperature monitoring of patients whenever “significant changes in body temperature are intended, anticipated, or suspected.” This includes most cases. The core temperature may be measured in four locations: pulmonary artery, nasopharynx, distal esophagus, and tympanic membrane. Bladder and rectal temperatures are not technically core temperature measurements but are appropriate in most cases. In the first hour of anesthesia, redistribution of cool blood from the skin to the core is responsible for the initial drop in core temperature. Prewarming the skin with warmed blankets or, more effectively, a forced-air warmer can prevent this initial drop in temperature. Warming the ambient temperature is the most important factor in reducing heat loss after the initial redistributive heat loss in the operating room. Heat loss from the skin is proportional to exposed skin, so covering as much exposed skin as possible helps to prevent heat loss. A heat and moisture exchanger can be used to minimize evaporative losses from ventilation. The most effective way of rewarming a patient, whether inside or outside the operating room, is a forced-air warmer. The warming of hypothermic patients should continue in the PACU. While forced-air warmers are the most effective method, warm blankets may be used for patients with mild hypothermia. Before discharge from the PACU, patient temperatures should be warmer than 36°C, and they should feel comfortably warm.
rationales:
Although they are commonly used in pediatric anesthesia, heat-moisture exchangers have little effect on the temperature of adult patients, whereas a forced-air warmer can significantly improve a patient's intraoperative temperature.
Answer C: Warm blankets are useful to cover areas of the patient, thus preventing exposed skin, but they lose warmth as the operation continues and can not actively warm the patient.
Answer D: Using cooled or room-temperature fluids for resuscitation may cause temperature loss, but using warmed fluids can only prevent a drop in temperature. This method is not as effective as forced-air warming for warming a patient.
bottomLine: Forced-air warmers are the most effective way to raise a patient's temperature in the preoperative, intraoperative, or postoperative setting.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Hypothermia: Prevention (B)" Barash PG, et al. Clinical Anesthesia. Commonly used monitoring techniques. 8th ed. E-book. Page 724. Sessler DI. Perioperative heat balance. Anesthesiology. 2000 Feb;92(2):578-96.

stem: Which of the following increases minimum alveolar concentration of inhaled anesthetics?
explanation: The minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) of inhaled anesthetics is increased by use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOI). Many factors decrease the MAC of anesthetic agents including acute ethanol ingestion, pregnancy, metabolic acidosis, and hyponatremia. Other factors include increasing age (especially > 40), hypoxia, hypothermia, induced hypotension, anemia, and certain drugs including α-2 agonists, lithium, large doses of cholinesterase inhibitors, lidocaine, opioids, barbiturates, and calcium channel blockers. By contrast, there are fewer factors that increase MAC. These include hyperthermia, hypernatremia, chronic ethanol abuse, and increased central neurotransmitter levels (e.g., as caused by MAOIs, acute amphetamine use, cocaine, ephedrine, and levodopa). In general, those factors that decrease central nervous system (CNS) metabolic activity, neurotransmission, CNS neurotransmitter levels, and down-regulate CNS responses to chronically elevated neurotransmitter levels decrease MAC. Those factors that increase CNS metabolic activity and neurotransmission, CNS neurotransmitter levels, and up-regulate CNS responses to chronically depressed neurotransmitter levels increase MAC. Answers A & B & D & E: Many factors decrease the MAC of anesthetic agents including acute ethanol ingestion, pregnancy, metabolic acidosis, and hyponatremia.
bottomLine: Hyperthermia, hypernatremia, chronic ethanol abuse, and increased central neurotransmitter levels (e.g. MAOIs, amphetamine, cocaine, ephedrine, and levodopa use) increase MAC requirements for anesthetic agents.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "MAC / Factors That Increase, Decrease" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 424-425.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is undergoing a craniotomy and anterior communicating artery aneurysm ligation under general anesthesia, with electroencephalographic (EEG) monitoring. Which of the following is TRUE regarding the changes seen on EEG with increasing depth of anesthesia?

options.text: Isoflurane at 1.0 MAC results in an EEG pattern indistinguishable from surgical levels of general anesthesia obtained with a propofol infusion
options.html: Isoflurane at 1.0 MAC results in an EEG pattern indistinguishable from surgical levels of general anesthesia obtained with a propofol infusion

options.text: Isoflurane below 1.0 MAC will generate an EEG pattern known as burst suppression
options.html: Isoflurane below 1.0 MAC will generate an EEG pattern known as burst suppression

options.text: Propofol for induction produces a low amplitude, high-frequency gamma and beta oscillations (25 to 35 Hz) at the time of loss of consciousness
options.html: Propofol for induction produces a low amplitude, high-frequency gamma and beta oscillations (25 to 35 Hz) at the time of loss of consciousness

options.text: Propofol infusions for general anesthesia produces a high power in the slow-delta (0 to 4 Hz) and alpha (8 to 12 Hz) range and lower power in beta and gamma range
options.html: Propofol infusions for general anesthesia produces a high power in the slow-delta (0 to 4 Hz) and alpha (8 to 12 Hz) range and lower power in beta and gamma range

explanation: The density spectral array will reveal high power in the slow-delta (0-4 Hz) and alpha (8-12 Hz) range and lower power in beta and gamma range with a propofol infusion at surgical levels of general anesthesia. The unprocessed electroencephalogram (EEG) result is the graphical representation of oscillatory local field potentials, measured at the scalp. The geometric organization of pyramidal neurons in the cortex facilitates the generation of large extracellular currents and local field potentials, easily recorded through the skull and scalp. Subcortical regions generate smaller field potentials, at varying geometric orientation and at a greater distance from the scalp, that make it difficult to record and characterize their activity on EEG. However, cortical and subcortical structures are richly interconnected, and subcortical structures influence the activity of cortical regions so that the EEG pattern recorded at the scalp reflects the states of both cortical and subcortical structures. Different anesthetic agents act at specific molecular targets and through distinct neural circuits producing characteristic changes in cortical and subcortical activity. These anesthetic-induced changes in brain electrophysiology, observed in the form of unprocessed EEG recordings, are reflective of the depth of anesthesia achieved by particular agents. The density spectral array is the two-dimensional representation of the decomposition of the raw EEG signal into the power content for each given frequency component. Propofol acts through postsynaptic γ-aminobutyric acid A (GABAA) receptors, increasing the chloride conductance and hyperpolarizing the postsynaptic membrane. Propofol enhances GABAergic inhibition of cortical pyramidal neurons by cortical inhibitory interneurons; it also enhances GABAergic inhibition from hypothalamic preoptic area projections to brainstem arousal centers and reduces thalamocortical excitatory input through augmentation of GABAergic inhibition at the thalamic reticular nucleus. Hyperpolarization of cortical pyramidal neurons and reduction of the subcortical excitatory input explain the slow and delta oscillations (0-4 Hz) seen on EEG. At low infusion rates of propofol and mild to moderate levels of sedation, the EEG tracing is dominated by organized, regular beta-gamma oscillations (25-35 Hz) with a larger amplitude than gamma oscillations in the awake EEG and greater frontal coherence. Bolus administration of propofol for induction of general anesthesia results in predictable changes in the EEG tracing, with a transition from the awake pattern of low amplitude beta-gamma oscillations to high amplitude slow-delta and delta oscillations (0-4 Hz) that correlates with loss of consciousness, apnea, and atonia. Repeated propofol boluses can convert the pattern of slow oscillations into burst suppression. Elderly (> 65 years) patients can enter burst suppression with standard induction doses of propofol. After the induction dose of propofol, the EEG transitions into a combination of slow-delta and alpha oscillations (0-4 Hz and 8-12 Hz, respectively) that correlates with a surgical plane of general anesthesia. The density spectral array makes this signature signal easy to recognize as a high power in the slow-delta (0-4 Hz) and alpha (8-12 Hz) range and lower power in beta and gamma range. Propofol infusions at an adequate rate for maintenance of general anesthesia preserve the characteristic EEG tracing with combined slow-delta and alpha oscillations. Isoflurane and the other volatile anesthetics achieve their physiological and clinical effects through mechanisms that are not fully understood. Multiple potential target sites have been identified through the brain and spinal cord. Volatile agents enhance GABAergic inhibition at cortical and subcortical levels, block two-pore potassium channels and hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated channels, and act as antagonists at N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors. Isoflurane at sub–minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) produces EEG tracings that resemble those of propofol, with slow-delta and alpha oscillations, providing evidence that enhanced GABAergic inhibition may be its dominant mechanism of action. At MAC of isoflurane and above, a large amplitude theta oscillation appears (5-8 Hz), which may reflect its non-GABAergic mechanisms. The density spectral array pattern of evenly distributed power, from the slow through the theta and into the alpha range, is unique to volatile agents at or above MAC. Higher concentrations of isoflurane starting at 1.5 MAC achieve burst suppression on EEG. Burst suppression is an EEG pattern characterized by periods of isoelectric quiescence interspersed with periods of high-voltage activity with preserved spectral content within burst periods. Burst suppression correlates with a state of maximal reduction in neural activity and cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen.
rationales:
Isoflurane at sub-MAC produces EEG tracings that resemble those of propofol, with slow-delta and alpha oscillations. At MAC of isoflurane and above, a large amplitude theta oscillation appears (5-8 Hz). The density spectral array pattern of evenly distributed power from the slow, through the theta and into the alpha range, is unique to volatile agents at or above MAC.
Answer B: Higher concentrations of isoflurane, starting at 1.5 MAC, achieve burst suppression on EEG.
Answer C: Bolus administration of propofol for induction of general anesthesia results in predictable changes in the EEG tracing, with a transition from the awake pattern of low amplitude beta-gamma oscillations to high amplitude slow-delta and delta oscillations (0-4 Hz) that correlates with loss of consciousness, apnea, and atonia.
bottomLine: Different anesthetic agents act at specific molecular targets and through distinct neural circuits producing characteristic changes in cortical and subcortical activity. These anesthetic-induced changes in brain electrophysiology, observed in the form of unprocessed electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings, provide evidence of the depth of anesthesia achieved by particular agents. explanationHtml:
The density spectral array will reveal high power in the slow-delta (0-4 Hz) and alpha (8-12 Hz) range and lower power in beta and gamma range with a propofol infusion at surgical levels of general anesthesia.

The unprocessed electroencephalogram (EEG) result is the graphical representation of oscillatory local field potentials, measured at the scalp.

The geometric organization of pyramidal neurons in the cortex facilitates the generation of large extracellular currents and local field potentials, easily recorded through the skull and scalp.

Subcortical regions generate smaller field potentials, at varying geometric orientation and at a greater distance from the scalp, that make it difficult to record and characterize their activity on EEG.

However, cortical and subcortical structures are richly interconnected, and subcortical structures influence the activity of cortical regions so that the EEG pattern recorded at the scalp reflects the states of both cortical and subcortical structures.

Different anesthetic agents act at specific molecular targets and through distinct neural circuits producing characteristic changes in cortical and subcortical activity.

These anesthetic-induced changes in brain electrophysiology, observed in the form of unprocessed EEG recordings, are reflective of the depth of anesthesia achieved by particular agents.

The density spectral array is the two-dimensional representation of the decomposition of the raw EEG signal into the power content for each given frequency component. Propofol acts through postsynaptic γ-aminobutyric acid A (GABAA) receptors, increasing the chloride conductance and hyperpolarizing the postsynaptic membrane.

Propofol enhances GABAergic inhibition of cortical pyramidal neurons by cortical inhibitory interneurons; it also enhances GABAergic inhibition from hypothalamic preoptic area projections to brainstem arousal centers and reduces thalamocortical excitatory input through augmentation of GABAergic inhibition at the thalamic reticular nucleus.

Hyperpolarization of cortical pyramidal neurons and reduction of the subcortical excitatory input explain the slow and delta oscillations (0-4 Hz) seen on EEG.

At low infusion rates of propofol and mild to moderate levels of sedation, the EEG tracing is dominated by organized, regular beta-gamma oscillations (25-35 Hz) with a larger amplitude than gamma oscillations in the awake EEG and greater frontal coherence.

Bolus administration of propofol for induction of general anesthesia results in predictable changes in the EEG tracing, with a transition from the awake pattern of low amplitude beta-gamma oscillations to high amplitude slow-delta and delta oscillations (0-4 Hz) that correlates with loss of consciousness, apnea, and atonia.

Repeated propofol boluses can convert the pattern of slow oscillations into burst suppression. Elderly (> 65 years) patients can enter burst suppression with standard induction doses of propofol.

After the induction dose of propofol, the EEG transitions into a combination of slow-delta and alpha oscillations (0-4 Hz and 8-12 Hz, respectively) that correlates with a surgical plane of general anesthesia.

The density spectral array makes this signature signal easy to recognize as a high power in the slow-delta (0-4 Hz) and alpha (8-12 Hz) range and lower power in beta and gamma range.

Propofol infusions at an adequate rate for maintenance of general anesthesia preserve the characteristic EEG tracing with combined slow-delta and alpha oscillations. Isoflurane and the other volatile anesthetics achieve their physiological and clinical effects through mechanisms that are not fully understood.

Multiple potential target sites have been identified through the brain and spinal cord.

Volatile agents enhance GABAergic inhibition at cortical and subcortical levels, block two-pore potassium channels and hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated channels, and act as antagonists at N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors.

Isoflurane at sub–minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) produces EEG tracings that resemble those of propofol, with slow-delta and alpha oscillations, providing evidence that enhanced GABAergic inhibition may be its dominant mechanism of action.

At MAC of isoflurane and above, a large amplitude theta oscillation appears (5-8 Hz), which may reflect its non-GABAergic mechanisms. The density spectral array pattern of evenly distributed power, from the slow through the theta and into the alpha range, is unique to volatile agents at or above MAC.

Higher concentrations of isoflurane starting at 1.5 MAC achieve burst suppression on EEG. Burst suppression is an EEG pattern characterized by periods of isoelectric quiescence interspersed with periods of high-voltage activity with preserved spectral content within burst periods.

Burst suppression correlates with a state of maximal reduction in neural activity and cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen.

stem: Which of the following changes in metabolism occurs in the setting of fasting and insulin deficiency?

options.text: Use of amino acids by the brain for energy
options.html: Use of amino acids by the brain for energy

explanation: The main feature of insulin deficiency is the disruption in protein balance, which can lead to emaciation and wasting. Muscle protein degradation (proteolysis) is increased as amino acids are delivered to the liver and kidney to be used as substrates for gluconeogenesis. During the first 24 to 48 hours after cessation of nutrient intake, glycogenolysis occurs to provide glucose to the tissues. Glycogenolysis is stimulated by insulin deficiency and an increase in glucagon. This increased glucagon to insulin ratio also promotes gluconeogenesis (endogenous glucose production). Hypoglycemia is further prevented by increased catecholamine release secondary to beta-adrenergic stimulation, which accelerates lipolysis. Lipolysis leads to the breakdown of stored triglycerides in adipose tissue into glycerol and free fatty acids (FFA). In the setting of insulin deficiency and the lack of glycogenolysis, FFAs undergo hepatic conversion to ketone bodies (eg, beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate), which are used as energy stores. The glycerol released during lipolysis and lactate produced by glycolysis are two substrates used for gluconeogenesis. As starvation continues, skeletal and smooth muscles undergo proteolysis into amino acids. Alanine and glutamine are among the amino acids transported to the liver, but some amino acids are transported to the kidney as substrates for gluconeogenesis. The brain adapts to low glucose availability by using ketone bodies for energy. Simultaneously, adenosine triphosphate is produced via the oxidation of FFAs released by lipolysis.
rationales:
In prolonged fasting and insulin deficiency, lipolysis is stimulated by catecholamine release via beta-adrenergic stimulation. Lipolysis leads to the breakdown of stored triglycerides into glycerol and free fatty acids.
Answer B: Glycogenolysis, not glycogenesis, occurs in the setting of insulin deficiency. As glycogenolysis decreases due to depleted glycogen stores, free fatty acids undergo hepatic conversion to ketone bodies used by the brain for energy.
Answer D: The brain does not use amino acids for energy. Rather, ketone bodies are formed by the conversion of free fatty acids by the liver, which are then used by the brain for energy in the setting of fasting and prolonged starvation.
bottomLine: In the setting of insulin deficiency, glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis are stimulated by an increase in the glucagon to insulin ratio. Hypoglycemia is further prevented in the setting of fasting by an increase in lipolysis via beta-adrenergic stimulation. The acceleration in lipolysis leads to the release of glycerol and free fatty acids from the breakdown of stored triglycerides in adipose tissue. Proteolysis is increased in prolonged starvation as amino acids are transported to the liver and kidney to be used as substrates for gluconeogenesis.

stem: According to the American Heart Association, which of the following defines the blood pressure cutoff value?
explanation: Blood pressure *For Hypertensive Emergency, there also needs to be evidence of new or worsening target organ damage. Blood ejected from the left ventricle into the aorta leads to a peak pressure, termed the systolic pressure. When pressure falls within the aorta, this nadir is the diastolic pressure. The difference in these two pressures is what is known as the pulse pressure. As the pulse pressure moves distal to the heart, the systolic pressure rises while the diastolic pressure falls, thus creating a larger pulse pressure. Physiologically speaking, mean arterial pressure is determined by the cardiac output (CO), systemic vascular resistance (SVR), and central venous pressure (CVP). The mathematical relationship between these factors is as follows: MAP = (CO * SVR) + CVP. The AHA also defines severe hypotension as SBP < 70 mmHg and suggests using medications such as norepinephrine, particularly for low total peripheral resistance.
rationales:
The AHA does not provide MAP criteria for hypertension.
Answer B: Hypertension is defined as BP > 130/80 mmHg, or 140/90 mmHg by some sources (e.g. JNC).
Answer C: The AHA defines hypotension as MAP < 65 mmHg, which is also the cutoff value used by the Surviving Sepsis Campaign.
bottomLine: Hypotension is commonly defined at SBP < 90 mmHg or MAP < 65 mmHg. Hypertension is defined as BP > 130/ 80 mmHg, with severe hypertension (hypertensive emergency) defined as BP > 180/110 mmHg.

stem: An otherwise healthy 17-year-old basketball player presents for an ankle external fixation after a sports injury. The patient desaturates after extubation due to prolonged laryngospasm, requiring administration of propofol and succinylcholine and reintubation. Pink, frothy sputum is suctioned from the patient's endotracheal tube during transfer to the intensive care unit postoperatively. Which of the following would be MOST expected on chest imaging for this patient?

options.text: Bilateral fluffy infiltrates on chest x-ray
options.html: Bilateral fluffy infiltrates on chest x-ray

explanation: Laryngospasm in otherwise healthy, young individuals is the most common cause of negative pressure pulmonary edema (NPPE). On a chest radiograph, NPPE would present as bilateral fluffy infiltrates. Negative pressure pulmonary edema occurs as a result of exaggerated negative intrathoracic pressure. Negative intrathoracic pressure increases right ventricular return, increasing the hydrostatic pressure gradient in the pulmonary vasculature while simultaneously increasing left ventricular afterload, further worsening pulmonary pressures. As a result, fluid moves from the pulmonary capillaries across the vascular bed and into the pulmonary interstitium and alveoli. Negative pressure pulmonary edema can be caused by any cause of upper airway obstruction (eg, biting on an endotracheal tube, laryngospasm, etc) but is most common in patients who are young and/or muscular because these patients can generate a stronger negative inspiratory force. Negative pressure pulmonary edema typically presents as dyspnea with pink-frothy sputum and bilateral fluffy infiltrates on chest images. Treatment consists of breaking the obstruction (ie, treatment of laryngospasm) and applying positive pressure ventilation (PPV) with supportive therapy. For some patients, NPPE will resolve within hours, but other patients require 12 to 48 hours of treatment and may require administration of furosemide. Chest radiograph of bilateral pulmonary infiltrates illustrating typical radiographic findings from NPPE.
rationales:
Pneumothorax is not associated with laryngospasm or NPPE.
Answer C: Pleural effusions are not a typical finding of NPPE.
Answer D: Right lower lobar infiltrates would be more consistent with lobar pneumonia, which is not part of NPPE.
bottomLine: Laryngospasm is the most common cause of negative pressure pulmonary edema, which is most common in patients who are young, healthy, and strong because these patients can generate the greatest negative inspiratory force. Negative pressure pulmonary edema occurs due to negative inspiratory pressure generated by inspiratory effort against an upper airway obstruction, which increases right ventricular return and left ventricular afterload, causing hydrostatic pressure in the pulmonary vasculature to increase and drive fluid from the pulmonary capillaries into the alveoli and interstitium. Negative pressure pulmonary edema presents with dyspnea, pink and frothy sputum, and bilateral fluffy infiltrates on a chest radiograph. Treatment is supportive with positive pressure ventilation, after which many patients recover quickly. Other patients may require furosemide administration.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding the rate of induction of anesthesia in the setting of intracardiac shunts is TRUE?

options.text: Inhalational induction is more rapid with a left-to-right intracardiac shunt
options.html: Inhalational induction is more rapid with a left-to-right intracardiac shunt

options.text: Inhalational induction is slowed with a right-to-left intracardiac shunt
options.html: Inhalational induction is slowed with a right-to-left intracardiac shunt

options.text: Intravenous induction is more rapid with a left-to-right intracardiac shunt
options.html: Intravenous induction is more rapid with a left-to-right intracardiac shunt

options.text: Intravenous induction is slowed with a right-to-left intracardiac shunt
options.html: Intravenous induction is slowed with a right-to-left intracardiac shunt

explanation: Inhalational induction is delayed in the setting of a right-to-left intracardiac shunt. The rate of inhalational anesthetic induction is determined by minute ventilation, functional residual capacity, blood/gas solubility, cardiac output, cerebral blood flow, and the presence of intracardiac shunts. A right-to-left intracardiac shunt delays inhalational induction since the volatile anesthetic-rich blood returning to the left heart is diluted by volatile anesthetic-poor systemic venous blood from the right heart. In addition, the uptake of inhaled anesthetics is prolonged with a right-to-left shunt due to a decrease in pulmonary blood flow. The chart below shows a summary of the various shunts and how anesthetic agents are affected.
rationales:
The rate of inhalational induction is virtually unchanged in the setting of left-to-right intracardiac shunting.
Answer C: The rate of intravenous induction in the setting of left-to-right shunt is decreased minimally, or not changed at all, due to increased recirculation of drugs into the pulmonary circulation.
Answer D: Intravenous induction is accelerated in the setting of right-to-left intracardiac shunting due to a partial bypass of the pulmonary circulation.

stem: Which of the following types of cells helps to prevent atelectasis?
explanation: Type II pneumocytes in the alveolus have a primary function of producing surfactant, which helps to prevent atelectasis. Secondarily these cells may also differentiate into Type I pneumocytes, which then contribute to gas exchange at the alveolar surface. At the cellular level, an alveolus is composed of Type I pneumocytes which give structure to the unit. Additionally, these cells lining the alveolus contribute directly to air exchange and diffusion to gases to and from the bloodstream. Type II pneumocytes are also present in the alveolus and produce surfactant, which helps to prevent atelectasis. In the event that the alveolus is damaged, Type II pneumocytes can also differentiate into Type I, and therefore contribute to gas exchange. A final type of cell in the alveolar unit is the alveolar macrophage, a phagocytic cell that helps to clear debris and microbes from the pulmonary system.
rationales:
Alveolar macrophages are primarily involved with consuming and clearing debris from the pulmonary system. This includes foreign particles such as dust and tar, as well as microbes.
Answer B: Endothelial cells, as part of the pulmonary vasculature, are involved with the passive diffusion of gases from the alveolus into the bloodstream, but are not directly part of the alveolus and do not produce surfactant.
Answer C: Type 1 pneumocytes arrange to form the structure of the alveolus and directly contribute to gas exchange. However, these cells are not capable of producing surfactant, which helps to prevent atelectasis.
bottomLine: Type 2 pneumocytes in the alveolus have a primary function of producing surfactant, which helps to prevent atelectasis. Secondarily these cells may also differentiate into Type 1 pneumocytes, which then contribute to gas exchange at the alveolar surface.
references: ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. “Respiratory Physiology: Lung Cellular Processes” West's Respiratory Physiology: The Essentials, Chpt. 1 "Structure and Function," pg. 10.

stem: Which of the following is the thermal neutral zone (TNZ) for a naked, full-term newborn?
explanation: For a naked, full-term newborn the thermoneutral zone is 32-35degC. Our bodies produce heat as a function of our metabolic rate. For an unclothed adult, when room temperature is between 26-28degC (50% relative humidity, still air), known as the thermoneutral zone, heat loss matches heat production from basal metabolic rate. More specifically, within that range heat loss occurs without sweating (e.g. dry or nonevaporative heat loss) and only depends on vasomotor tone; there may be less vasodilation at 26degC than at 28degC, but the body is not required to produce more heat than simply that of basal metabolic rate. Below the thermoneutral zone, normothermia can be maintained by increasing metabolic rate. Well-trained young adults can increase their basal metabolic rate up to five times their basal rate and avoid hypothermia with room temperatures as low as 5degC. Conversely, when temperature is higher, normothermia can initially be maintained by evaporative heat loss. Thus, a more complete and precise definition of the thermal neutral zone is “the range of ambient temperature at which metabolic rate is at a minimum, and within which the temperature regulation is achieved only by control of sensible ('dry' or 'nonevaporative') heat loss, that is, without regulatory changes in metabolic heat production or evaporative heat loss.” The thermoneutral zone for a naked, full-term newborn is 32-35degC. Below this, thermogenesis will increase metabolic rate, but only up to 2-3 times, and will only avoid hypothermia with room temperatures above 23degC. In small premature infants (1 kg), the lower limit of the thermoneutral zone may be as high as 35degC. Answers A & B & C: The thermoneutral zone for a naked, full-term newborn is 32-35degC.
bottomLine: The thermal neutral zone is the temperature at which normothermia is achieved with basal metabolic rate. For a naked, full-term newborn the thermoneutral zone is 32-35degC.
references: Fetal and Neonatal Physiology, 4th edition, chapter 58, 624-648 Clinical Anesthesia, 7th edition, Chapter 41, 1199-1200 ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Neonatal Physiology: Thermal Regulation Neutral"

stem: What is the principal extracellular electrolyte and what hormone mediator controls its total body content?
explanation: The principal extracellular electrolyte is sodium, a cationic element found in the body. Its total body content is controlled by both aldosterone and atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP). This differs from anti-diuretic hormone (ADH), which alters the concentration of sodium in the body. Conditions upon which both aldosterone and ANP are released differ, but both alter total body sodium. When blood volume or systemic pressure decrease, aldosterone is released. Aldosterone functions in the renal distal tubules to increase the absorption of sodium. ANP is released in response to increased blood volume, sensed by the atrium myocytes, and causes a decrease in total body sodium leading to decreased blood volume. Answers A & B: Potassium, nor calcium, is not the principal extracellular electrolyte; its homeostatic mechanism is not determined by ANP.
rationales: While sodium is the principal extracellular electrolyte, ADH dictates the concentration of sodium and not the total body content.
bottomLine: The adrenal cortex is stimulated to release aldosterone by a decrease in fluid volume, a decrease in systemic pressure, and from beta1 stimulation.
references: ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. “Renal Physiology: Extracellular Fluid” Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 7th edition. Page 210 and 341

stem: An obese 50-year-old man is undergoing laparoscopic prostate surgery. To improve surgical visualization, the surgeon asks for steep Trendelenburg positioning. After this change, you note the following changes over a 20-minute period: His blood pressure cuff is on the upper arm and the ventilator remains in pressure control mode. What is the most likely cause of his hypoxemia?
explanation: Laparoscopic insufflation causes a decrease in diaphragmatic excursion simply by increasing intra-abdominal pressure. If the ventilator settings are not changed, the tidal volume will decrease leading to CO2 retention and hypoxemia. Most patients require an increase of 30% in minute ventilation to counter the increase in CO2 from insufflation. Physiologic changes that take place during insufflation include: - Decreased lung compliance and increased inspiratory pressure, due to an increase in intra-abdominal pressure and Trendelenburg position. - Increased ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch, due to atelectasis and decreased functional residual capacity (FRC). - Elevated CO2, due to CO2 insufflation and decreased lung perfusion and ventilation. Most patients require an increase of 30% in minute ventilation to counter the increase in CO2 from insufflation. A modest increase in inspiratory pressures is needed to counter the reduced lung compliance and FRC associated with pneumoperitoneum.
rationales:
Hypercarbia needs to be significant before oxygenation is affected to this degree.
Answer C: Compression of the inferior vena cava (rather than the superior vena cava) would cause a decrease in preload and resultant hypotension, but would not cause hypoxemia.
bottomLine: Laparoscopic insufflation causes a decrease in tidal volumes when using pressure-control ventilation. Hypoxemia can be due to atelectasis and decreased diaphragmatic excursion.
trueLearnInsight: During laparoscopic procedures, it is best to use either volume-control or pressure-control volumeguaranteed modes of ventilation. Pressure control alone can assist with achieving appropriate tidal volumes, but at the risk of over-ventilation with position changes and desufflation.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. “Laparoscopy: Hypoxemia (B)” Complications in Anesthesia. 2nd Ed. pp 831 - 835.
